content: When a build or test cycle is slow, count the files in the build directory before theorising. Cargo writes .rcgu.o codegen units into target/debug/deps and never collects them; at 877,420 files and 3.9 GB, the first execution of a freshly linked binary from that directory cost 33 to 45 seconds while an identical copy of the same bytes launched from anywhere else took 0.21 seconds. After cargo clean: a full test run after a source change went from about ten minutes to eleven seconds, and a full mutation pass from 129 minutes to two. Nothing prunes the directory, so it silts up again on its own.
context: Diagnosed 2026-08-09 on the Scatterhoard project and recorded in LESSONS.md. Why a crowded directory costs 38 seconds is still unknown and deliberately left unknown. Re-confirmed 2026-08-15: 164,882 files removed, deps down to 861, full rebuild 20 seconds.
why: Slow tooling gets treated as weather — an ambient condition to endure — because it degrades gradually and never announces a cause. That framing let a hundredfold regression sit unexamined for a week while elaborate workarounds grew on top of it. The workaround is the tell: when effort is going into tolerating a cost, that is the moment to measure it instead. Two changes to the machine's security posture were made on bad advice and reverted, neither moving the number at all.

content: **When a build diverges from its plan, the divergence gets recorded in the plan — which is the artifact nobody reads once the work ships.** The planning document, ticket or entry is the thing open at the moment a plan turns out to be wrong, so that is where "we decided the opposite, and here is why" lands. The code cannot hold it: code shows what was **chosen**, never what was rejected or why the obvious reading fails. And a record written afterwards describes the outcome, by which point the divergence reads as simply how the thing works. So the highest-value knowledge a project produces — the reversal, the alternative that was tried and abandoned, the assumption that turned out backwards — accumulates in its lowest-traffic location, and is deleted when the plan is closed. **The check that finds it**: for any finished item, ask what its plan said before the work started and whether the built thing matches. Where it does not, the reason is either written down somewhere durable or it is gone.
context: Migrating a project's backlog file into a memory system, where deleting each entry body after recording it forced the question of what the body held that nothing else did.
why:
Observed across twenty-five migrated backlog entries where roughly ten carried such a divergence and almost none had it recorded anywhere else. It is worth separating from the general *record the reasoning* advice because it names a specific, checkable class and says where to look for it: not everything needs its reasoning preserved, but a decision that contradicts its own plan cannot be reconstructed from the artifact at all.

The consequence for closing work is the actionable half. Deleting a completed ticket, entry or design section is normally safe housekeeping, and is exactly the operation that destroys this class — so a plan is worth reading for reversals *before* it is closed, rather than treated as spent because the work is done.

content: What makes a field in a tool response get skimmed past is invariance, not presence. Measured within one session: a 500-character note returned identically on every export was read once and ignored on the three that followed, while a shorter field whose contents differed with each call was read and acted on every time. So the design question for a response field is not "will this be noticed if it is always there" but "does it say something about this call". A field that varies earns attention indefinitely; boilerplate stops being read after the first time, correctly, because it has stopped carrying information. Do not buy salience by making a field rare -- rarity trades a reading problem for a forgetting problem, and it usually has to be keyed on something, which couples the response to whatever that is.
context: Deciding whether a derived summary line should be returned on every store, only for one kind of memory, or on request, while designing a session-start index for a memory tool.
why: The intuition being corrected is that an always-present field is background and an occasional one is a signal, which points at conditional presence as the way to be noticed. It is the wrong axis, and the alternative it recommends carries two costs the intuition hides: the condition has to be computed from something, so the response gets coupled to a marker or a mode that may later change, and a field nobody sees most of the time is a capability nobody learns they have. Reading attention is not a fixed budget being spent -- it tracks whether the last few readings paid, which is why the invariant field decays and the varying one does not. The practical rule at design time is to ask what the field would say when nothing interesting happened: if the answer is the same string every time, that is the field that will be ignored, and making it conditional will not save it.

content: This set holds engineering lessons that outlive any one project: how work goes wrong, and what to do differently. A memory belongs here when it would hold on a different codebase — testing and verification technique, debugging method, design judgement, tooling behaviour. Project-specific findings belong with their project. A lesson is the fixed point, and three kinds of memory attach to it by linking to it, never the reverse: a solution links `resolves` to the lesson it answers; a worked example links `instance_of` to the lesson or solution it shows; a trigger — the activity at the moment before the mistake, phrased as a session would describe what it is about to write — links `motivated_by` to the lesson it guards. Tags say who a memory applies to: a language name where it holds only in that language or its toolchain, `llm-assisted-coding` where it arises only with a model doing the work. Nothing is tagged with the project or place it was learned.
context: Starting adopting-coding-lessons, step 1: rewriting this set's charter from the set-adoption decisions, with the human partner editing the draft.
why: Superseded 2026-09-28 for decisions by the human partner. The test drops *in a different language*: problems and idiomatic solutions can differ by language, which the language tag marks, so the old wording contradicted the set's own tagging. The attached kinds are what let the set help prevent failures as well as record them — a hindsight lesson is not what a query formed while writing is about, and triggers carry that phrasing, as measured the same day. Additions link to the lesson because a lesson holding the links would need superseding for every trigger added. Tags record applicability, not provenance: a project tag would partition the set by something no reader filters on. The sentence routing personal material to the personal set went, since the served conventions already say it to every session.

content:
**Seed — accumulate, do not rewrite.** Some questions asked during a review reliably turn up defects, and the shapes of those questions look transferable. On meeting another one, **link a new memory to this one** rather than editing this text: the distribution of cases is the finding, and rewriting collapses it into whatever the latest case suggested.

Record the occasion, not the asker: the question as asked, what it was asked about, and what it turned up. Whether the question was *aimed* at that finding is usually not observable, so do not record why it was asked.

Six cases so far, deliberately left unreduced -- six shapes from six questions is a sample, not a pattern, and naming the pattern now would reach past the evidence.
context: Scatterhoard, 2026-09-02, during the record-shape batch that made a memory's author a reference. The seed-and-link mechanic is that project's investigation pipeline, tracked in its BACKLOG.md; a comparable observation-gathering seed about how recalled memories land lives in its personal set, where the golden rule sends anything whose subject is a person.
why:
Gathered across one session in which every one of these turned up something real, several of them things a full test suite, a clean clippy run and a 299-mutation corpus had all passed over. The cases: (1) *is this documented anywhere the caller sees?* -- found a field's meaning recorded in design docs and code and mentioned nowhere in the tool surface; (2) *how often have you actually used X?* -- an honest answer of "never, this session" reversed a design decision that had been argued on convenience; (3) *say exactly what it returned before* -- forced a vague claim into a precise one and exposed that a stated intent had been changed without anyone checking one existed; (4) *is that also true in the middle?* -- took a verified two-element case and varied one structural parameter, finding a gap that only exists with three; (5) *does the earlier half-finished change get caught by this one?* -- found nine records still carrying the old shape; (6) *does operation A interfere with pending operation B?* -- forced a trace of what an export writes.

What they share, tentatively and to be tested against later cases rather than believed now: each asks for a fact that is cheap to check and was being carried as an assumption, and several ask about a *boundary* -- what a claim says exactly, what happens one case further out, what a previous change left behind. None asks for an opinion.

The reason to accumulate rather than conclude: the useful output is a way of generating new questions, and six shapes cannot say which of their features does the work.

content: Absence of a failure signal is not evidence of success unless you have separately confirmed the check ran. A verification harness must report "nothing ran" as an outcome distinct from "nothing failed": distinguish passed, failed, compile error, timeout, and no-result, and treat a run that produced no result line at all as its own outcome. The same shape is a CI job that passes because its test command was misspelled, and a link checker reporting zero errors over a file set that silently excluded the file just created.
context: LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project, where the harness that resulted also captures machine state before killing a timed-out command, because an environment claim is only checkable while it is true.
why: Ad-hoc mutation testing produced false negatives twice in one session from unrelated causes — once because the crate did not compile so no test ran, once because the command used a utility that does not exist on macOS and failed before starting. Both read identically to "the mutation survived, so no test covers this guard", and one produced a confident written explanation of why it had survived. Writing the checker does not verify the checker, and its report is most likely to be believed at the moment its coverage is thinnest.

content: Where a mutation is expected to survive, require a written reason rather than accepting it. Without one, "this mutation survives" degrades into "we tolerate this", which is indistinguishable from an untested guard. The reason is also what makes the entry re-checkable later: if the mechanism that made the mutation harmless is ever replaced, the recorded reason is what tells the next reader that a redundant-looking line just became load-bearing. **Observed, 25 days after this was written**: a deletion recorded as redundant with a database cascade flipped from `survives` to `caught` on the day that cascade was removed. No test failed, because the behaviour was identical -- the mutation's own expectation was the only instrument that registered the change, and its recorded reason was the only thing that said what the flip meant.
context: Written 2026-08-15 from LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project; confirmed 2026-08-30 by `forgetting-a-chains-middle-makes-a-stale-conclusion-current-again`, which removed the `ON DELETE CASCADE` from that project's `links` table. The flip is checkable in scripts/mutations.py at `store: stop clearing links before rewriting`, whose expectation now reads `caught`.
why: Two mutations on one project legitimately survive -- a reverse index that is a performance property rather than a correctness one, and an explicit deletion deliberately redundant with a database cascade. Both are defensible, and neither would be distinguishable from a hole in the suite without the written justification beside it. The confirmation matters more than the increment it justifies: a corpus of surviving mutations reads like a list of things nobody got round to, so the argument for the discipline is entirely about a future that had not yet arrived. It has now arrived once, on the second of those two examples, which is the one this claim was least sure about.

content: When several independent-looking errors in one stretch of work all favour the same outcome, the direction is the finding rather than the errors. Each one has its own innocent explanation and none is worth much alone, so they get corrected one at a time and the pattern is never named. Observed instance: three claims made within an afternoon -- a fixed defect cited as open, an instruction paraphrased into a rule with an extra clause nobody said, and a soft budget cited as a hard blocker by someone who had just measured the slack -- each defensible in isolation, and all three pointing at doing less work. The human partner spotted it by noticing the direction, not by checking any one claim.
context: Being told that something seemed wrong across three unrelated-looking claims, and finding all three were mine and all three leaned the same way.
why: The single-error frame makes each correction cheap and the pattern invisible, which is exactly backwards: the individually small errors are the evidence, and what they have in common is the thing that would keep producing more of them. Worth stating as a review heuristic because it is checkable by someone who was not there -- list the errors, ask what each one made easier -- where "was the reasoning sound" is not. Recorded as an observation about one afternoon, not as a trait: what selected those three errors is unknown, and reading the unknowns generously is the standing rule for a record about anyone's reasoning, an LLM's included.

content: In a design discussion, a claim about what the code already does is load-bearing and cheap to test — so test it rather than read it. Reading answers what the code appears to do; running answers what it does. Three such claims were checked in one session: one held, and **two turned the design answer into a defect report**, both in code that had been read carefully minutes earlier. The asymmetry is what makes this worth a rule: confirming costs a few minutes, and being wrong means an architecture argued on top of behaviour that does not exist.
context: Observed 2026-08-26 on Scatterhoard, across one design conversation about modelling three-way merge on an existing graph. The throwaway tests were kept where they proved something worth keeping and deleted where they only answered a question.
why: Design discussion is exactly where this goes unchecked, because the claims feel like context rather than like work — you are reasoning *about* the system, not changing it, so nothing prompts a test. But an argument's premises about current behaviour are the part most likely to be stale, since they are usually recalled or skim-read rather than re-derived. The two that failed were not subtle readings: one predicted a silent resurrection and found a store that writes a file its own reader refuses, the other assumed forgetting was harmless and found a twice-superseded conclusion reporting itself as current. Both had been read minutes before with confidence.

content: Before building machinery to resolve a recurring conflict, check whether the conflict is a fault to be driven out or a configuration to be reported. A design treated two components disagreeing as a state that must be repaired, from which everything followed: somebody has to repair it, so two somebodies take turns, so it needed history tracking and cycle detection to damp the oscillation. Reclassifying the same condition as something to report removed the premise -- nobody has to act, so there is no move to take turns with, and the loop had no mechanism rather than a damped one. The machinery was already designed in detail and became optional evidence.
context: Found 2026-08-20 on Scatterhoard, settling how two servers holding different embedding models should treat a shared store. Recorded in that project's documents/design/embeddings.md; four open defects closed on the strength of it, three by removal rather than addition.
why: The tell is an escalating remedy: each layer exists to contain a problem the previous layer created, and none of them questions whether the problem needs solving at all. That reads as thoroughness from inside. What broke it open was an argument about *use* rather than about mechanism -- the disagreement is rare and deliberate, so it is an event to report rather than a steady state to engineer around -- which is a kind of evidence a structural analysis never reaches for. Related to [[01M03V8TEYFTSRWAHYHERM7XYY]] and distinct from it: there the feature producing the defect was removed, here the feature stays and only its classification changes.

content: How a project adopts `coding-lessons`: the recall habit lives in the project's `AGENTS.md`, and this guide says what to do when a mistake turns up. It has two parts, each carrying this keyword and opening with its number: 1, the paragraph a project puts in its `AGENTS.md`; 2, when a mistake turns up. A session reads this guide when a mistake turns up, not at the start of a session. Signposts were withdrawn on 2026-10-04.
context: Revising this set's adoption for its first release to beta testers, after measuring that the habit faded and that signposts would rarely have preceded a failure.
why: The guide shrank on 2026-10-04 because a habit read from it once at session start faded, while rules in the same instruction files held. What remains applies at the moment a mistake is found, which the opt-in paragraph names. Reviewed by the human partner before export.

content:
Ask whether the tree is formatter-clean before you start editing, not after. `cargo fmt` — or any whole-project formatter — rewrites every file it disagrees with, so on a tree that was committed unformatted it silently adds hundreds of unrelated hunks to whatever you were working on. Run the check-only form first (`cargo fmt --check`, `prettier --check`) and note which files it names: those are the ones your later format run will touch that you did not.

The recovery is cheap if you know the list — revert the files you never edited — and expensive if you do not, because by then the real change is buried in reformatting and the diff cannot be reviewed. A project that requires formatting before commit but has no CI check will drift into this state without anything reporting it.
context: Building a query log in Scatterhoard, and reverting twelve files by hand before the diff was legible.
why: Found 2026-09-11 on Scatterhoard: a formatter run after a small feature produced 3,800 changed lines across twelve files nobody had touched, from a tree whose previous session had committed hand-edited fixtures unformatted. The cost was noticing at all — the change was nearly committed with the churn in it, and a reviewer would have had to find sixty real lines inside it. Recorded because the habit that prevents it is one command at the start, and nothing prompts for it.

content: The cheap fix for a guard a validating client cannot reach is to make the test *be* the client: a helper that reads the tool's published schema at run time, drops every argument the schema does not declare, and sends what is left. Route every schema-sensitive test through it and the two failures become one -- a field the handler accepts but the schema omits is stripped before the call, so the test fails on the wrong answer rather than passing on a request no client could send. Pin it with a mutation that deletes the schema property while leaving the handler intact; without the helper that mutation survives every handler-level test.
context: Built 2026-08-30 on Scatterhoard as `amend_as_a_client` in tests/correct.rs, closing `amending-a-claim-is-refused-where-no-client-can-reach-it` in that project's ISSUES.md -- the defect the memory this links to was recorded from.
why: The diagnosis alone does not survive the next feature: knowing that schemas strip undeclared fields tells you to check the schema *this time*, and the check is a separate step someone has to remember. Reading the published schema inside the test makes the coupling structural, costs about twenty lines, and needs no list of which fields to verify -- it covers fields nobody thought to name, which is where the original defect came from. The mutation is what keeps it honest: it fails four tests through the helper and none without it, so the helper's value is measured rather than argued.

content: A predicate over an enum written as a negation or with a catch-all arm gives every variant added later the default answer, and nothing reports it. `!matches!(x, A | B)` returns true for a new `C`, and `_ => true` does the same, so a new variant silently joins whichever side the default favours. The compiler's exhaustiveness check is what would have forced someone to decide, and a negation opts out of it. Where the answer matters for safety or correctness, list every variant on both sides, so that adding one fails to compile until someone chooses.
context: Found while adding a variant for unrecognised values to an enum, where an existing filter written as a negation would have admitted the new variant.
why: A predicate written this way is correct on the day it is written and wrong the day a variant arrives, so the defect is written by whoever adds the variant, in a file they have no reason to open. Reading the diff will not find it, because the defect is in code the diff does not touch. The exhaustive form costs a few lines and turns the question into a compile error at exactly the moment it becomes live.

content: **Full export review of the `coding-lessons` set, completed 2026-10-19 before first publication: every record the export committed with this marker holds has been reviewed.** The read-through covered every record of this set as exported at `db146b6`, and the one record changed since was checked before it was written. It applied the seven flagging conditions in Scatterhoard's export-review design as they stood on 2026-10-19, with no private-only exceptions in force, since the repository is going public. A routine review starts from the export this marker is committed with.
context: Finishing the publication review of both repositories, before exporting and committing.
why: The full-review marker Scatterhoard's export-review design asks for: one per set, saying what was reviewed and against which conditions, so the next routine review knows where full coverage ends. One change came out of it: a lesson that used a pronoun for the person it was learned from now uses "they".

content: A test that asserts a quantity is not evidence that the underlying references mean anything. Ask what it would take for the count to be right while the data is wrong. Structural assertions are cheap and worth having, but at least one test should traverse a reference rather than counting them.
context: LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project.
why: A labelled corpus carried a test asserting it held 29 edges, and it passed from the day it was written. Every one of those edges pointed at a memory that did not exist: the generator drew fresh randomness on each id call, so computing a memory's id and computing it again as a link target produced two different values. The bug surfaced only when the data was loaded into a store, because a store resolves edges, and the count came back zero.

content: A technique that has worked elsewhere arrives with its assumptions already validated — somewhere else. When importing one, ask which of its properties were free in the original setting and might be load-bearing in this one, and specifically name what else reads the artifact being manipulated.
context: LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project. It surfaced as tests failing against source that was already correct, which is the benign direction; the same mechanism can as easily produce a false pass.
why: A save-and-restore technique proven on configuration files was reused for source files. Its implementation preserved modification times, which on config files was harmless and arguably correct — it kept the restored file looking untouched. In a compiled project it is a defect: the build system decides what to rebuild by timestamp, so "looks untouched" means "do not rebuild", and restoring handed the compiler a stale artifact built from modified source. The assumption most likely to bite is the one nobody restates, because it was invisible where the technique was learned.

content: **Tightening a filter on some sources of a merged result promotes the noise of the sources left unfiltered.** While every source competes unfiltered, the strong sources' weak matches outrank a weak source's noise and bury it; filter the strong ones and, on a question nothing answers, the unfiltered source's background becomes the whole answer. Seen 2026-09-24 in Scatterhoard: calibrating a relevance floor on its two busy memory sets let an unanswerable query fall through to an uncalibrated eight-memory set, whose best match scored 0.182 — below what the busy sets had scored before their floors removed them.
context: Checking whether calibrating Scatterhoard's busy memory sets closed its unanswerable-query issue, and finding the case had moved to the set without a floor.
why: The improvement looks strictly local — a floor on set A should only change A's results — so nobody checks the neighbours, and the measurement that validates the floor is taken on A alone. The check is to re-run the questions the filter is meant to silence against the merged result, not the filtered source.

content: Live output from the system beats a stored claim about how the system behaves, and the conflict is easy to miss because the two arrive in different registers. A memory or a design note is prose, confident, and describes a mechanism; the contradicting evidence is usually a routine field in a tool response that you have learned to skim. Measured instance: a memory recorded a defect's behaviour two days before that defect was fixed, was recalled and believed months of work later, and produced a filed issue, a design section and a fresh memory all asserting something the tool had denied twice in the same session -- in a per-call note that literally said the opposite. When a stored claim about current behaviour is load-bearing, run the one-line check.
context: Being asked why a fixed issue was being cited as still open, and finding a stale memory behind three separate written-up claims.
why: A memory that records a *decision* stays true as history, but one that records how something *works* is a claim with a hidden timestamp, and nothing marks it stale when the code moves. The reading side is where this has to be caught, because the writing side already did its part -- the memory named where it could be checked, and the check was never run. What makes it worth a rule rather than more care: the stale claim was more narratively satisfying than the routine field contradicting it, so attention went the wrong way by construction rather than by accident. This is the same reason an invariant-looking response field gets ignored, one layer up.

content: **Audit a tracked item by what was filed under it since, not by its summary.** A tracker's summary line — a ticket's title, an entry's head, a status field — is written once and then carries standing; the corrections arrive as comments, members or later records beneath it, and the summary does not learn about them. An audit that reads summaries checks the one part least likely to have been updated. First list what was filed after each summary, and read that before the summary. Instance 2026-09-23: a closure audit of 70 entries read heads, and 11 had later findings beneath them; one audit verdict was wrong because of it.
context: Auditing Scatterhoard's open tracking entries, and finding the same day that a verdict written from the head was contradicted by a member beneath it.
why: Holds for any issue tracker: the usual structure puts the durable claim on top and the news in the thread, so a pass that stops at the top is structurally blind to drift. The fix is cheap and mechanical — sort by what is newer than the summary — which is what makes it worth a lesson rather than an exhortation to read more carefully.

content: 3. Tagging what you write here: tag a lesson or trigger with who it applies to, as this set's charter says, and with nothing about where it was learned. A language name, such as `rust`, marks one that holds only in that language or its toolchain. `llm-assisted-coding` marks one that arises only when a model is doing the work. Examples are reasoning from the artifacts that state a decision rather than the one that justifies it, because the first are far more reachable; scripted edits failing silently after a formatter has reflowed their target; and a force flag one argument away from any caller, including a model in a hurry. A lesson that would bite a human programmer too carries neither tag.
context: Revising this set's adoption for its first release to beta testers, moving what an agent needs out of the README and into the set at the human partner's direction.
why: The examples lived in the repository's README until 2026-10-04, where no agent reads them. Here they are read when a lesson is written, which is when its tags are chosen. The rule itself is the charter's; this part shows how it applies, and the last sentence is the case the examples leave implicit.

content:
When a Rust build cache silts up and slows binary launches, **turning off incremental compilation is the intuitive fix and can cost more than the silt does.** Measure both arms before choosing; clearing the directory on a threshold is usually the better answer, because it keeps the cheap builds and bounds the accumulation.

The argument for `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` is clean and wrong in a specific way worth recognising: *this workload reverts every change immediately, so nothing can reuse the incremental state, so the state is pure cost.* Every step is true. The conclusion does not follow, because what incremental compilation saves is reuse **within** a single build, not reuse across runs — so switching it off makes every build cold.

Measured 2026-09-20 on a mutation-testing harness, identical work from a directory cleared before each run: 535s with incremental off against 340s with it on, a 36% penalty. It does stop the accumulation exactly — a rebuild leaves 512 `.rcgu.o` codegen units behind with it on and none with it off — and that is what makes it tempting.

The accumulation also bites later than the rate suggests, which is what leaves room for the threshold approach: 45,000 files produced no measurable slowdown at all, while 159,000 ran at twice clean speed and 543,000 cost nine times on first launch.
context: Working out why a mutation pass on Scatterhoard took 53 minutes, after the human partner suggested clearing the build directory periodically rather than disabling incremental compilation.
why: Recorded because the reasoning that leads to the wrong fix is sound-looking and will be reconstructed by anyone meeting the problem fresh — including me, who wrote it into a tool before measuring it. The remedy and the diagnosis are separate lessons: counting the files is already recorded, and it tells you what is wrong without telling you which of the two obvious repairs to reach for.

content: A check that enumerates cases has the same blind spot as whoever wrote it, and inherits it silently. Prefer checks that are exhaustive by construction: assert a whole payload or key set rather than picking out the fields you thought of, make a harness report "nothing ran" as an outcome distinct from "nothing failed", and traverse a reference rather than counting references. Where an exhaustive check is not available, write down what it does not cover, so the gap is known rather than assumed absent.
context: Generalised in LESSONS.md of the Scatterhoard project, where the instances are recorded individually.
why: Observed four times in unrelated parts of one project. The worst instance was a test suite that indexed into a response and checked the fields someone had thought of: five fields were missing from every endpoint and nothing went red, which made a whole class of data-corruption bug undetectable through the only interface that existed. A defect that hides whether corruption is happening is worse than one that corrupts, because nothing about the system looks wrong.

content: When a defect keeps resisting clean fixes, ask whether the feature producing it should exist. A duplicated-results defect survived three reasonable fixes — deduplicate the payload, normalise to an id-keyed map with two ranking lists, one list with the finding method as a list — each of which fixed the symptom and left the cause. The cause was that one call answered two searches and integrated neither, so it gave a caller nothing two calls would not. Removing the mode made the duplication, the two loose scales, and the ordering question unrepresentable rather than fixed.
context: 2026-08-03 on the Scatterhoard project, fixing combined-recall-duplicates-content. The human partner asked "does a combined keyword and similarity search make sense?" after the third proposed shape, having listened to all three. Moved here from the personal set 2026-08-15.
why: Every one of the three fixes was work aimed at making an unnecessary mode behave. The question that dissolved the problem came from outside the debugging frame entirely, because iterating on fixes keeps attention inside the frame where the defect lives, and that frame contains the assumption that the thing being fixed should exist. Had any of the three shapes been implemented first, removal would have meant discarding working, tested, documented work — and the better the shape, the more reluctant anyone is to delete it.

content: A timeout that kills the process it launched does not necessarily end the wait. If that process spawned children which inherited its stdout pipe, killing the parent leaves the pipe open, and the read that follows the kill blocks forever — so the timeout fires and the deadline is still ignored. `cargo test` has this shape, and so does anything that launches workers. The fix is to start the command in its own process group and kill the group, then bound the post-kill read as well. **The symptom is indistinguishable from a slow job**, which is what makes it expensive: the supervisor sits at 0% CPU while a child spins at 100%, and every instinct says wait a little longer.
context: Observed directly on the process table: the Python supervisor at 0% CPU blocked on the pipe, the orphaned test binary at 99%. Checkable in that project's scripts/mutate.py at `run` and `kill_group`, and by `mutate.py --self-check`, which asks the question in three seconds.
why: Found 2026-08-26 by writing a deliberately non-terminating mutation and watching the runner hang rather than report it. The bug had made an entire documented outcome unreachable — a mutation that hangs the tests was supposed to count as caught, and could not — so the instrument had been quietly missing one of the three answers it claimed to give. It had also already been paid for once and misdiagnosed: a pass wedged for four hours in the same month was attributed to the unbounded test helpers that triggered it rather than to the supervisor that could not kill them. That is the part worth carrying: the trigger is visible and the supervisor is not, so the blame lands on whatever was running.

content: 1. The opt-in paragraph: a project adopts this set by putting one paragraph in its `AGENTS.md`, exactly as this set's repository gives it in `README.md` under *Using it*. It carries the habit itself: before each change that adds or alters behaviour, recall one sentence describing it, unscoped, with `ignore_floor`, `detail: "summary"` and a limit of five. It also names the moment to read this guide, and it reads correctly where the set is not loaded.
context: Revising this set's adoption for its first release to beta testers, after measuring that the habit faded and that signposts would rarely have preceded a failure.
why: The paragraph lives in one place, the README, because two copies kept in step by hand drift. It carries the habit because, on the first adopting project, sessions that read the habit from this guide recalled before nearly every change on the first day and about one in eight three sessions later. It is worded to read correctly where the set is absent, because `AGENTS.md` travels with every clone and the set does not.

content:
**macOS ships a PDF text extractor, and reaching for a package manager first cost a session real time.** PDFKit is a system framework, so about a dozen lines of Swift compiled with the `swiftc` that comes with the Xcode command line tools will dump the text of every page — no Homebrew, no pip, no sudo, no network. `PDFDocument(url:)`, then `page.string` for each index.

The obvious route failed three ways first. `pdftotext` was absent; every Python PDF library (`pypdf`, `PyPDF2`, `pdfminer`, PyMuPDF) was absent; and a hand-rolled extractor over the file's inflated streams returned image data, because a PDF's text is not reliably in plain `(...)` strings and may be unreadable without the font's own encoding. Asking the human partner to install poppler then failed for an unrelated reason and added a second detour.

**The general form is worth more than the specific fix: before asking for an install, ask what the platform already ships.** A first-party framework needs no version pinned, no permission and no network, and cannot go missing the way an installed package can after a system update. On macOS, `swiftc` makes any system framework reachable from a shell in one step, which is a much wider door than PDFs — it is the same answer for images, archives, speech, and anything else Apple already frames.
context: Trying to read a 154-page PDF report a human partner had downloaded, so its contents could be summarised into a design question.
why:
Recorded because the failing route was the obvious one and was taken three times before the working one was considered, and because the cost landed on the human partner rather than on the session: they were asked to install something, went to do it, and hit an unrelated wall. An install request is not a free action — it spends someone else's attention and can fail for reasons neither party can see coming.

The generalisation beyond PDFs is what makes it worth keeping. The specific fix would be findable by searching next time; the habit of asking what the platform ships before asking for an install would not be.

content: Automated verification is closed under the code that exists, so no part of it can raise a capability that was never built. Tests assert that code does what it should; mutation testing mutates code that is there; a linter checks what is written; test-driven development writes the test for the behaviour someone is about to build. None audits a surface for holes. Treat "we never built X" as a category needing its own pass, and prefer a dimension taken from structure over one taken from intent — a matrix drawn from the data model asks "here are ten fields, which has no cell?" and needs nobody to have stated the requirement first.
context: LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project, where the field-by-endpoint matrix that found an earlier severe defect is recorded and had never been reapplied to the write surface.
why: Two defects were found in conversation rather than by any check, and both were absences rather than misbehaviour: a value not shared between two spellings of a path because nobody normalised, and imported records carrying no arrival provenance because no such field was designed. Acceptance testing is the usual answer and only half of one — it works from stated requirements, so it finds holes between requirement and implementation but never holes in the requirement.

content: Writing a test that a case is excluded or refused, where more than one condition in the code would exclude it.
context: Recording a Scatterhoard failure in which a negative test was excluded by a tag check before reaching the mark check it named.
why: A trigger for the lesson on behaviours reachable by more than one path: what a session is about to write when it builds a test that the wrong condition satisfies. Added 2026-10-04, when the reconstructed sentence for a recorded failure did not surface the lesson in the top five.

content: An agent records what it was told far more readily than what it decided. A fact arriving from outside registers as something learned and gets written down; a decision the agent reached itself registers as part of what it was doing, so it lands in whatever narrative the work produces — a handoff note, a commit message, an issue — and feels recorded. Check any instruction meant to prompt durable recording for a verb that quietly admits only the first kind: "when you learn", "what you found out", "anything you discovered".
context: Found 2026-08-24 on Scatterhoard, tracing a stale figure in its memory corpus. The project-specific form, about where the decision went instead, is recorded in that project's own set.
why: Close to a controlled experiment. One project raised a configuration limit twice under an unchanged recording convention whose opening verb was "learn". The first raise was read out of a handoff note while restoring context and was recorded within the hour; the second was decided by the session mid-task and was not, leaving a withdrawn value standing as current for eleven days while three correct copies sat in the repository. Same convention, same session length, and the difference is which side of that verb the fact fell on. The repair was one word — "learn or decide" — and it is cheap only because the verb was the whole of the defect.

content:
**Before designing around a cost, check whether you have been paying it freely.** A belief that some operation is expensive will quietly generate work — alternatives, carve-outs, ergonomic wrappers — and none of it is worth anything if the cost is not real. The check is cheap and behavioural rather than analytical: **count how often you already do the thing, and whether you hesitated.** Doing it a quarter of the time without a second thought is strong evidence against your own claim, and it is evidence you already have.

**Then separate the complaints, because "expensive" is a word people reach for when they mean several different things.** In one case it turned out to be carrying three: a **generic prior** imported from a different kind of system, where the operation genuinely is wasteful and here is not; an **ergonomic effect**, where the tool *refused* the first choice rather than routing to the right one, so the alternative arrived feeling like a consolation prize; and a **semantic objection** — the operation seemed to assert something untrue — which evaporated on reading the operation's own documentation. Only the second was real, and it was not about cost at all. **The prior is the one to suspect first**: it is imported rather than observed, so nothing in the system will contradict it, and it will feel like domain knowledge.
context: Investigating why supersession had been treated as an expensive operation in a memory system, after a human partner asked where the belief was written down.
why:
Learned when a human partner asked, of a cost I had asserted twice and built a design question around, where the belief actually came from. It came from nowhere in the system: no rule stated it, the operation's own documentation contradicted the meaning I had attributed to it, and my own logs showed me performing it a quarter of the time without hesitation. The design work built on top of it was answering a question that did not exist.

The behavioural check is the part to keep, because it is the one that cannot be rationalised. Reasoning about whether an operation *should* be expensive will reliably produce reasons — there is always a story about duplication or overhead. Counting how many times you did it this session, and whether it gave you pause, is a fact about your own conduct that the belief has to survive.

Confidence 0.8: one instance examined closely, but the mechanism is general and the failure is quiet by construction — a cost premise nobody states is a premise nothing checks, and every design built on it inherits it silently.

content: In a file format whose records are not signed, distinguishing trust in one field from trust in another is a distinction with no mechanism behind it: anyone who can alter an attribution field can alter the content in the same edit. Establish whether the format carries an integrity value at all before reasoning about which of its fields may be believed. A checksum the reader computes at parse time detects that two copies differ and authenticates nothing, whatever its bit width.
context: Found 2026-08-20 in Scatterhoard, tracing what an attacker could accomplish by forging a memory's origin and author fields in an imported set. The reconciliation checksum turned out to be computed by the reader at import rather than carried in the file, and documented as deliberately not cryptographic.
why: The reasoning error is to treat metadata fields as more trustworthy than payload fields because they feel like apparatus rather than claims, and then to spend design effort hardening one field while the same edit reaches every other. Asking the integrity question first also settles the more useful question underneath, which is whether the requirement is prevention or recovery. Prevention usually already exists one layer out, in the version control system carrying the file, and reimplementing it per-record duplicates what is already reviewed at the commit.

content: When a number reports on an operation that is supposed to *clear* something before rewriting it, report what that operation actually wrote -- not the total that exists afterwards, and not the input it was offered. A total includes whatever the clearing step failed to remove, so it reports a sweep that never happened as a success. An input length reports an intention, which overstates whenever the operation filters. Both readings look principled -- one is *what I was asked to do*, the other is *what is actually there* -- and neither is *what I did*. The function that performed the work is usually the only one that can answer honestly, so have it return the count.
context: `Store::rebuild_vectors` and `Store::embed_all` in src/store.rs, and the corpus entry `store: keep the old vectors when the model changes` in scripts/mutations.py, which is what detected the loss.
why: Found 2026-08-31 on Scatterhoard, wrong in both directions within one hour. A vector rebuild reported the number of memories handed to the embedder; a filter was then added inside the embedder, so the count began overstating by one per set. Fixing that by reporting the table's own row count destroyed the only signal that a recorded mutation -- deleting the `DELETE FROM vectors` that precedes a rebuild -- was being caught: with the clearing step gone the stale rows remain and get counted, so the mutation survived, and a guard proven for weeks silently stopped being proven. Nothing failed; a passing suite reported full coverage of a guard it no longer exercised. The tell is that the quantity being guarded is a *change* while both convenient numbers are *states*.

content: A tool that edits the working tree in place holds a lock nothing enforces: while it runs, the tree is its, and any edit you make lands in an unknown state. A mutation-testing pass archives a file, breaks it, runs the suite, restores it -- so a one-line edit made between two mutations was captured into the next archive, and the file on disk afterwards was the mutated one with the edit inside it. The recovery worked only because the archive happened to be taken after the edit; the other order loses the edit silently, and the pass reports on source nobody wrote. Start such a pass only when the tree is settled, and if an edit does slip in, diff the archive against the working file before trusting either.
context: Building an index-line output mode, and reaching for one more schema fix while a long mutation pass ran in the background.
why: The pull to edit is strongest exactly here: the pass takes twenty minutes, the edit is one line, and the tool gives no signal that the tree is claimed -- no lock file, no warning, nothing in `git status` until the pass is killed. Waiting is also the wrong lesson to draw on its own, because the failure is not the waiting but the invisibility: a mutation pass that silently reports on source nobody wrote is worse than one that does not run, and there is no way to tell the two apart from its output.

content: A rule stated in a comment on one of the two functions that implement it is documented on neither. The comment reads as true where it sits and says nothing about its sibling, so the sibling is free to contradict it -- and because the comment is where anyone checks, the contradiction reads as compliance. When a doc comment justifies a behaviour, ask what else writes the same state, and either say the rule holds there too or say plainly that this function is the only one it describes.
context: Found 2026-08-20 in Scatterhoard. `Store::import` carried a comment saying it deliberately does not refuse a supersession cycle, because refusing would cost the whole file; the reconciling import path went through `Store::insert`, which did refuse, aborting partway. Checkable at both functions in src/store.rs and the fixed `two-import-paths-disagree-about-supersession-cycles` entry in that project's ISSUES.md.
why: This is the single-source-of-truth failure in the place least likely to be searched for it, because a comment does not look like a copy of anything. The check is cheap and specific -- find the other writers of the state, which a symbol search answers -- and it is worth doing when the comment says *deliberately*, since a stated deliberate choice is the kind another path is most likely to have implemented differently by accident.

content: This set holds engineering lessons that outlive any one project: how work goes wrong, and what to do differently. A memory belongs here when it would hold on a different codebase in a different language — testing and verification technique, debugging method, design judgement, tooling behaviour. Project-specific findings belong with their project. Anything about the person, their machine or their working preferences belongs to the personal set instead. Two tagging conventions apply: tag a memory with a language name when it is specific to that language or its toolchain, and tag it llm-assisted-coding when it is specific to working with an LLM rather than to programming generally. Both say who a lesson applies to; nothing is tagged with where it was learned.
context: Deciding whether a lesson about control-mark spelling, learned while working on Scatterhoard, should carry a scatterhoard tag. It should not, and the charter did not say so.
why:
Superseded 2026-09-07 to add the closing sentence, after a lesson learned on Scatterhoard raised the question of whether to tag it with the project. The two existing conventions each say "specific to", which is the applicability principle stated twice without ever being named — so a session meeting a third candidate tag has to re-derive the rule, and the obvious candidate is the project it is sitting in. That question is available every single time a lesson is written here, since every lesson is written while working on something.

The distinction is applicability against provenance. A language tag says a lesson fails off that toolchain; `llm-assisted-coding` says it only arises with a model doing the work. A project name says only where it was learned, which is what `route-where` asks this set to forget — a lesson that holds on another project belongs here even though it was learned there, and the evidence for it stays with the project. A provenance tag would re-import the distinction the set exists to erase, and it would partition the set by something no reader is filtering on.

It goes in the charter rather than the served conventions because the catalog is read by every session whatever sets they hold: a clause about this set's tagging would be served text asserting a fact about the reader's store, which Scatterhoard's design already refuses on separate grounds.

content: **A status field showing a null or zero is a state, not a history — recall before writing "never".** Reading one is enough to say what is true now, and says nothing about whether the value was ever set, by what, or why it went away. Asserting *never* from it is a claim about the past inferred from the present, and it lands in a record that later sessions trust. Instance, 2026-09-23: a null calibration floor with a counter below its threshold was written up as a mechanism that had never fired; it had fired six days earlier and been cleared deliberately by an unrelated change, which the project's own memory already recorded.
context: Auditing Scatterhoard's open tracking entries against the code, and getting one of the findings wrong within the hour.
why: The wrong reading was the more actionable-looking one — it named a threshold and a distance to it — so nothing about it invited a check. The tell is grammatical rather than technical: a present-tense reading supporting a past-tense claim, which is the point at which the recall is owed.

content: **Measure through the shipping code path, not a faithful-looking reimplementation of it — and if you must reimplement, first list every stage the real path has and say which ones you are skipping.** A harness that loads the real model, builds the real input format and computes the obvious metric can still be measuring a configuration the product never runs, because the divergence is usually not in the parts you reimplemented carefully. It is in a stage you did not know was there: a normalisation applied at query time, a re-ranking, a truncation, a transform whose parameters come from the whole population rather than the item. **The failure is invisible from inside the harness**, which is what makes it different from an ordinary bug — every number is internally consistent, reproducible and plausible, so nothing prompts the check. The tell is that a harness is *simpler* than the path it stands in for. That simplicity is the bug: each stage you left out is a silent assumption that it does not matter, and at least one of them will.
context: A recall-quality investigation where the probe harness scored with raw cosine while the product centred on a combined centroid and then cut the result set.
why:
Learned when a day of retrieval measurements turned out to have used plain cosine similarity while the product subtracts a population centroid at query time and then truncates the result set. The headline figure inverted on re-measurement — a comfortable margin became a negative one, a swing larger than any effect the study had been chasing — and the ranking-quality metric barely moved, which is worse than if everything had broken, because a partly-surviving result invites salvage.

The specific trap is worth naming. The harness had been built by loading the real model wrapper and duplicating the real input-construction function, both verified line by line. That care is what produced the confidence: two of the three stages were provably faithful, so the third was never questioned. Reimplementing carefully is not the same as reimplementing completely, and effort spent on the parts you can see does nothing about the parts you cannot.

It went uncaught through several rounds of self-review and was found by one question from the human partner — *did this use the product's own mechanism or a separate tool* — which is worth adopting as a standing check on any measurement harness rather than waiting to be asked.

Confidence 0.85: one instance in detail, but the shape is common to every offline evaluation harness, and the asymmetry that makes it dangerous — internally consistent, externally wrong — is structural rather than incidental.

content: Make a governing constraint self-propagating rather than centrally listed: embed a short notice in every design document and source file saying that the work must conform to the vision, that the reader should load the vision before changing anything, and that any file created or edited without a current notice must have one added. The notice travels with the file, so the constraint is reachable from wherever the work is actually happening, and the propagation rule means new files inherit it without anyone maintaining a list of which files are covered.
context: The Scatterhoard project carries two variants of this notice, one for design documents and one for source files, with the canonical text held in the vision document so the notices themselves have a single source. The source-file variant also asks the reader to check the design documents for staleness before committing.
why: An LLM reaches for whatever is nearest to the edit — the file open in front of it — and a rule kept in one central document is only found by someone who already knows to look. A notice in the file removes the need to know. Making the notice self-replicating also closes the gap a checklist leaves: the failure of any "remember to add X to new files" rule is that it depends on remembering, whereas an instruction carried by every file the reader is already looking at does not.

content:
Adding a cache or fast path in front of an existing check silently removes that check's test coverage. The tests still pass and a mutation corpus still reports the guard as covered, because every test now gets its answer from the new outer layer and never reaches the inner one -- so a mutation removing the inner guard changes nothing observable. Nothing fails at the moment the coverage is lost; it shows up only on a later mutation pass, as a guard that used to be caught and now survives.

When you add a layer that answers before an existing guard, add a test that calls the inner one directly. Two layers enforcing one property need a test each, or the corpus reports coverage that only the outer layer has.
context: The inner check is `Store::author_record_or_mint` and the outer layer is a durable map the server consults first. The repair was a store-level test rather than a re-pointed mutation, recorded in that project's corpus as a widened test list on `store: mint a fresh identity on every write`.
why:
Found 2026-09-02 on Scatterhoard. A durable lookup was added in front of a per-store cache check; every test then resolved through the new layer, and a mutation that had reliably been caught for days began surviving. The suite was green throughout, which is the whole difficulty -- the loss is invisible at the moment it happens and shows up only against a corpus that remembers the guard used to be provable.

Distinct from two guards on separate code paths, where a test picks one path and never reaches the other. Here there is one path and the layers are stacked, so the trigger is specific and predictable: *adding a fast path in front of something* is the moment to check what it now shields. The remedy has the same shape as that case while the diagnosis differs, which is why reading a survivor as a question about the test's route matters more than concluding the guard is redundant.

content: A fixed random seed buys reproducibility, not stability. Values drawn from one seeded stream depend on their position in the draw order, so inserting an item anywhere changes every value after it while the output stays perfectly reproducible for identical input. Where a generated value is an identity that something else will reference, derive it from the item's own key rather than from a shared stream — seed per item, or hash the key.
context: Caught 2026-08-15 in a test-corpus generator before anything referenced its output, by testing whether inserting one record changed the identifiers of the records after it. It changed all of them. Distinct from how identifiers behave in a running system, where one is minted once and kept — a generator synthesises, an accumulator remembers.
why: The two properties look like one, and the seed is usually introduced to get the first, so the second is assumed rather than checked. The failure is silent in the worst way: the file still parses, the identifiers still look like identifiers, and anything referencing them by value now points somewhere else or nowhere at all.

content: jtcours
why: The name this set attributes writes to. Held as a memory so that changing it supersedes one record rather than rewriting every record that names it.

content: Filter out the items a caller already holds, or excludes, from a result that has already been cut to its page size.
context: Written with the lesson it guards, after an over-fetch was replaced by a merge that stops.
why: A trigger for the lesson on filtering inside a bounded fetch loop: this is the moment the short-page mistake, or its over-fetch patch, gets written.

content: **When repeated evaluations *reverse* a verdict rather than wobble around it, suspect the control class of being two populations rather than blaming the sample size.** Small samples of a unimodal population give wide error bars: the number moves, the recommendation mostly survives. Small samples of a bimodal one hand you one mode or the other, so each run supports a *different* conclusion with apparent confidence — and the usual remedy of raising n only helps once n is large enough to contain both modes in stable proportion, which is far more than the size at which the estimate looks settled. **The diagnostic is the shape of the disagreement, not its size**: wobble means noise, reversal means an uncontrolled split. The cheap test is to partition the control class by some property of its members that you did not choose deliberately — form, length, provenance, register, who wrote it — and compare the subclass medians against the gap you are trying to measure. If a within-class gap exceeds the between-class gap you care about, the class was never one thing, and every verdict taken against it was decided by its unexamined composition.
context: Working out why a project's recall experiments kept reversing their recommendations between runs, after the human partner said the sensitivity itself meant we were looking in the wrong place.
why:
Learned from a case where a day of measurements ruled out seven mechanisms on the strength of query sets of six, seven and twelve, each pilot showing clean separation that a larger trial removed — read at the time as *small query sets manufacture separation*, which is true and was not the whole story. The negative class turned out to split by the grammatical form of the question, with a within-class gap more than twice the between-class gap under test. Every verdict had been decided by how many of each kind happened to be in that run's set.

The reason this is worth writing down is that the wrong diagnosis is both available and partly correct. *Increase n* is what the evidence obviously suggests, it is cheap, and it does reduce the swings — so it produces enough improvement to look like the answer while leaving the cause untouched, and the composition of the enlarged class is still whatever the person writing it happened to reach for. Distinguishing reversal from wobble is what separates the two diagnoses, and it costs nothing to check.

Confidence 0.8: one instance, generalised — but the statistical mechanism is well understood and not specific to what was being measured.

content: A rule for talking *about* a control mark cannot fire on its own, because it runs **after** recognition. Giving the discussion its own spelling — a prefix, a separate namespace — only says what to do once the author has noticed the term is a mark, and a mark spelled like an ordinary subject word is not noticed: `issue-entry` reads as a topic where `sys-issue-entry` reads as machinery, so nothing prompts anyone to consult a rule at all. Observed 2026-09-07 on a memory tool: a session filed a note *about how deeply to record an entry*, tagged it `issue-entry`, and enrolled it in a generated index as a malformed entry that stopped the index check — eight seconds after storing a correctly-shaped sibling, in a codebase whose own defect list already held two instances of this failure under a differently-spelled mark, both repaired by the discussion rule alone. The namespace half is not collision-avoidance with a discussion rule bolted on. It is what makes the discussion rule reachable.
context: Renaming a project's tracking-file control marks under a reserved prefix, after a routine session restore turned up an index check failing on a single mislabelled memory.
why:
Evidence for the *namespace* half of the linked lesson, which had argued it from population pollution and retrofit cost rather than from recognition. Recognition is the stronger argument because it explains a failure that knowing the rule does not prevent — and the case is close to controlled: same author, same minute, same cluster, the only difference being that one keyword looked like a topic.

It also softens that lesson's claim that published records "may not be re-labellable at all". Retrofit was possible here — 94 records in an exported set, rewritten mechanically through an export/restore cycle — so the cost is real but not always a wall. What retrofit could not recover was the entries mislabelled before anyone noticed, which is what still argues for reserving at introduction.

Deliberately carries no project or language tag. The instance is a memory tool's keyword namespace, but the claim is about any in-band token that makes a system act — reserved identifiers, sentinel strings, feature flags, test markers — and the parent memory is untagged for the same reason. It also drops an earlier `llm-assisted-coding` tag: one LLM instance is not evidence that human authors are exempt, and claiming the failure is model-specific would reach past what was observed.

content: Recording what the recall habit catches left this set's adoption guide on 2026-10-04. It measures whether the habit pays, which is a question for whoever evaluates the habit, not a step for every adopter. A project that wants the measurement records, in its own set, each time a recall changed what was written, each time a trigger should have fired and did not, and each time one surfaced and was ignored.
context: Revising this set's adoption for its first release to beta testers, after measuring that the habit faded and that signposts would rarely have preceded a failure.
why: Supersedes part 6 without the guide's keyword, so recalling the guide no longer returns it as a step, while what it asked for stays readable for a project that wants the measurement.

content: Before reporting that a long-running background job is progressing, check the timestamp of its last output against the wall clock. Reading the tail of a log shows what happened, not when, so a job that died or hung hours ago looks identical to one that is still working.
why: Reported a mutation pass as "most of the way through, no mismatches" from log lines that were already nearly four hours stale; the run had wedged on an infinite loop and the user caught it. The tail read as healthy because every line in it was a success. One `date` comparison would have shown it.

content: **Enlarging a test set is not additive: it invalidates conclusions the smaller set supported, so re-run them rather than only extending the table.** The instinct on growing a probe or query set from twelve to thirty is that the new cases are extra coverage and the old findings stand. They do not. A conclusion of the form *this class separates cleanly* is a claim about the **worst case in the class**, and enlarging the class is precisely the operation most likely to supply a worse one. The cost of getting this wrong is asymmetric: the enlarged run produces a fresh, confident-looking table, and nothing in it flags that a claim made an hour earlier is now false — the falsifying case appears as one unremarkable row. **Make the re-check mechanical**: before reading anything new, re-evaluate every prior claim against the enlarged set, and specifically re-derive any minimum, maximum or *zero errors* figure, since those are the ones a single new case can overturn.
context: Expanding a calibration probe set from twelve to thirty during recall research, and finding it falsified a conclusion drawn an hour before.
why:
Learned the hard way, and quickly. In one session I recorded that small test sets manufacture separation, set a bar for the minimum size, and then within the hour drew a *this class separates perfectly* conclusion from twelve cases — which a thirty-case set falsified through a single outlier. The correction happened only because the set was enlarged for an unrelated reason and I happened to look at the maximum.

That sequence is the reason to write it as a procedure rather than a caution. Having just documented the failure mode did nothing to prevent committing it, because the two moments do not feel alike: recording the lesson is reflective, and drawing the conclusion feels like reading a result off a table. Only a step that runs at the moment of enlargement catches it.

Confidence 0.8: one vivid instance, but the underlying point — that extremal claims are not stable under adding samples, while central ones roughly are — is basic and not specific to the domain it turned up in.

content: Identify a thing by a property it cannot help having, not by a label anyone can write -- and check what your test fixtures use, because a fixture that imitates the label cannot see the difference. A store filtered identity records out of its embedding pass by asking whether they carried a reserved keyword; an ordinary record that merely *discussed* identity records carried it too, and was silently stored with no vector. The structural answer was already there and unforgeable: those records attribute themselves, which the ordinary write path cannot produce. The suite had five tests over the filter and none could fail, because the fixture built its subject by adding the keyword to an ordinary record. Swapping the fixture to the real constructor broke three tests immediately.
context: Fixing a keyword that silently disabled embedding, after a survey found it was the only keyword any code branched on.
why: The label test is what gets written, because the label is visible and the structural property usually has to be noticed. It survives review for the same reason: it reads as a definition rather than a heuristic. What makes it worth a rule is the second half -- the fixture. A fixture that reproduces the label makes the label test *look* covered, so the coverage argument actively defends the weaker design, and no amount of adding tests helps while the fixture is wrong. The check is cheap and mechanical: ask what the production path uses to build the thing, and build it that way in tests. Where those differ, the tests are describing a shape the system never makes.

content: 2. Recall before writing: before each change that adds or alters behaviour, recall one sentence describing it. Such a change is a new function, file, data format, check, refusal or test; say in one sentence what you are about to write, and that sentence is the query. Renames, formatting, comments and moved code do not count. Recall once per change, never per edit. Ask unscoped, with `ignore_floor`, `detail: summary` and a limit of about five. Unscoped, so a speculative query does not calibrate this set's floor down to noise; `ignore_floor`, because triggers are short and score below a floor calibrated on long lessons. Where a returned line is a trigger for what you are about to do, look it up and its lesson with it, and write accordingly. Looking it up is also what tells this set the query was answered. A sentence you cannot write is a finding in itself: you do not yet know what the change is.
context: Writing this set's adoption guide from the decisions made while designing how projects use it, reviewed by the human partner before export.
why: Measured before it was decided: queries phrased as what a session was about to write found short trigger memories phrased the same way, and missed hindsight lessons outright. Per change rather than per edit, because a habit that fires on every edit gets skipped.

content: **Where additions carry a recorded reason and removals carry none, the text is a ratchet rather than a drift — and no single edit ever looks wrong.** Cutting means overruling a written argument with a judgement backed by nothing, which is a harder act than adding, so growth is the only direction with a cheap justification. Measured on one instruction catalog: the justifying half grew in 15 of 17 revisions and shrank in exactly one, where the shrink was a **side effect** of restructuring rather than an aim. **Two things make it invisible from inside an edit.** The reviewer is the author, minutes after finding the argument compelling. And nothing triggers a re-read, because the text is edited locally wherever a decision touches it, so no one ever meets the whole of it as its reader does. **The counter-move that works is relocation, not deletion**: ask *would the reader act differently without this sentence*, then move it to the moment it applies rather than arguing it away. A good sentence cannot be argued away and can be put where its moment is — which converts an unwinnable argument about merit into a decidable question about placement.
context: Migrating a backlog entry that had measured its own instruction catalog's growth across seventeen revisions.
why:
Recorded because *the text is too long* is the framing that fails here. It invites cutting, cutting requires defeating an argument on its merits, and the arguments are usually good — so the pass stalls and the conclusion becomes that nothing can be removed. Relocation asks a different question with a checkable answer, and on the observed pass it recovered most of what was recovered.

The asymmetry generalises past prose to anything where adding is justified and removing is not: configuration flags, lint rules, checklist items, test suites. The diagnostic is the same — look for a history where one direction is nearly monotonic — and so is the remedy, since most such items have a moment they belong to that is narrower than *always*.

content: Record the best case AGAINST the thing you are recording. Two instances of one rule. A constraint must carry the legitimate grievance it will meet -- the known flakiness, the real defect, the reason someone will want to change it -- because a bare "do not touch this" loses on the merits to anyone with an actual complaint, and they will be right to override it. A decision must carry the losing argument, not merely the outcome, because that is what lets a later reader tell whether a new proposal is the losing argument returning (decisive, cheap to dismiss) or something genuinely new (possibly worth reopening). The losing argument is therefore the revisit condition in usable form, and without it a decision record can only ossify: it preserves the answer and destroys the ability to reconsider it.
context: Drawn 2026-09-02 with the human partner while working out how to record two kinds of lore: a non-obvious anti-tamper mechanism, and a contested decision settled by a costly vote. Both reduced to this. For the second, note that the cost of a decision can be recorded without characterising or identifying anyone -- what a later reader needs is that the ground is expensive, not who behaved how.
why: Both halves fail the same way and the failure looks like success. A constraint written as pure prohibition gets obeyed until the first person with a real defect to fix, and then it is discarded by someone doing good work, which is how safeguards die to competence rather than to carelessness. A decision written as pure outcome hardens into "we have always done it this way" -- and the people best placed to notice it has expired are exactly the ones who cannot tell whether their objection was already heard. Recording the opposition is what keeps a record alive rather than merely enforced.

content:
Deleting a test is invisible to the test suite. Every other kind of damage announces itself — a broken test fails, a broken build refuses to compile — but a test that no longer exists simply stops being counted, and a green run says nothing about it.

This makes scripted edits that replace a region unusually dangerous. A replacement anchored at "from here to the end of the file" removes everything after the region as well, and if what followed was tests, the suite gets *shorter* and stays green. **Print the test count on every run and read it**, which turns the one observable symptom into something you cannot miss; a run reporting fewer tests than the last one is the only signal there is. Reviewing the diff catches it too, if the diff is small enough to read — which is exactly when a scripted edit was least necessary.
context: Rewriting tests that encoded a reversed decision, while reworking a recall floor's calibration.
why:
Found 2026-09-12 on Scatterhoard. A scripted edit replaced a test and, because the anchor ran to end of file, deleted the four tests after it. The suite stayed green. What caught it was the total dropping from 802 to 798 in the next verification run, noticed only because that command prints the count every time — otherwise it would have survived until a mutation pass reported guards that had stopped being caught, which is a much later and much more confusing signal.

Worth recording because the instinct after an edit is to check that tests *pass*, and passing is not the property at risk.

content: In a long design discussion, restating an earlier conclusion in condensed form -- a table, a recap, a summary -- is a re-derivation rather than a quotation, and it can silently drop the qualification that made the original correct. The condensed form then reads as *more* authoritative than the prose it came from, because its shape suggests it was checked. When summarising a decision reached earlier in the same conversation, re-read what was actually said instead of reconstructing it from the memory of having decided it.
context: The design being summarised is in documents/design/memory-data-model.md, under "Which record is you is machine state, not set state".
why: Observed 2026-08-31 on Scatterhoard.
