A two-level cache had been worked out several turns earlier: a per-set cache read on every write, backed by a durable table consulted only on a miss, split precisely so the durable copy stayed off the write path. A summary table drawn later collapsed it to one level, showing the durable table consulted on every write -- contradicting the reason for the split. The human partner caught it by asking. The tell is that the original reasoning was correct, still available, and unchallenged by anything in the intervening conversation: the error entered at the summarising step alone, which is exactly where nobody is looking, because a summary is taken for a record of a decision rather than a fresh claim about it.

content: Scripted string-replacement patches against source code fail silently once a formatter has reflowed the code the find-string was written against. Three failed in one session; two mattered, and each left a feature half-implemented in a way that only surfaced later as behaviour making no sense. Prefer an edit tool operating on freshly read text, and verify a patch landed by grepping for the new text rather than trusting a success message.
context: 2026-08-05/06 on the Scatterhoard project, implementing tombstones across three files, with cargo fmt as the formatter. Moved here from the personal set 2026-08-15.
why: A replacement whose pattern does not match is a no-op, not an error, so the failure is invisible at the point it happens. The risk rises sharply once a formatter runs between writing the pattern and applying it, which is exactly what happens in a session that formats after each change.

content: How a project adopts `coding-lessons`: the recall habit lives in the project's `AGENTS.md`, and this guide says what to do when a mistake turns up. It has three parts, each carrying this keyword and opening with its number: 1, the paragraph a project puts in its `AGENTS.md`; 2, when a mistake turns up; 3, tagging what you write here. A session reads this guide when a mistake turns up, not at the start of a session. Signposts were withdrawn on 2026-10-04.
context: Revising this set's adoption for its first release to beta testers, after measuring that the habit faded and that signposts would rarely have preceded a failure.
why: The guide shrank on 2026-10-04 because a habit read from it once at session start faded, while rules in the same instruction files held. What remains applies at the moment a mistake is found, which the opt-in paragraph names. Part 3 was added the same day, moving the tagging examples out of the README, which no agent reads. Reviewed by the human partner before export.

content: When you change how a value is spelled, every detector keyed to the old shape stops recognising it -- and whether that failure is loud or silent is a property of the detector's design, not of the change. Changing an id's encoding broke three at once. A mutation runner announced `find text is not in store.rs` and stopped. A test-snapshot normaliser, which matched the old shape to replace per-run ids with stable tokens, simply stopped matching: it wrote raw ids into every snapshot, so the files would have churned on every run afterwards. Grep for what *recognises* the old form, not only for what *produces* it.
context: Found 2026-08-20 on Scatterhoard, moving memory ids from hex UUID to Crockford base32. A third instance the same day: an error message that quotes its bad input put a per-run value into a snapshot, which is the same class arriving from the output side.
why: Producers are easy to find because they fail to compile; recognisers are pattern-matchers over strings and keep running happily against input they no longer understand. The contrast between the two failures is the transferable part: the runner compared against a literal it expected to find and could therefore report its own staleness, while the normaliser's miss looked exactly like "there was nothing to normalise here". A recogniser that cannot tell absence from non-recognition will always degrade quietly, which is worth knowing when writing one, not only when changing one.

content: Once text that a model's safety classifier flags has entered a coding session's context, every later request in that session can be refused, whatever the new message is — so the refusals look like they come from whatever ran last. Load sensitive source material (a threat report, a dual-use paper) in a separate session and bring back only the analysis you need, rather than extracting the whole document into the working session. When refusals start following harmless output, suspect earlier context before the latest command, and start a new session instead of retrying or switching models.
context: Diagnosing why the previous Scatterhoard session kept blocking. That session added the golden-rule-beyond-person-harm open question from Anthropic's September 2026 threat-intelligence report, then built summary.rs. This session re-ran the full test suite and read the old transcript with flightlog.
why: Observed in Claude Code on 2026-09-12/13 (flightlog session 71864250-2159-4671-9a04-ec6a602cb2a0). Earlier in the session, all 154 pages of a threat-intelligence report were extracted into the scratchpad and read, including its section on biological misuse. From 05:31 UTC onward, requests were refused with "Details: [bio]" right after unrelated tool output: a snapshot review, a keyword grep, `ls`, and a line reading "832 passed, 0 failed, 54 ignored". To the human partner it looked like test output was triggering the block. Switching from Opus 5 to Opus 4.8 did not help, and neither did deleting the scratchpad files, because the text was still in context. A fresh session ran the same `cargo test` with no refusal. That the context caused the refusals is inferred from this pattern; the classifier's reasons are not visible, hence 0.7.

content: A check run at small scale tests whether something is expressible, not how it performs. At a few dozen records every schema, index and scan performs identically, so a benchmark there measures noise and calls it evidence. What such a check can establish is whether a query is expressible, whether an invariant is natural to maintain, and whether references resolve. Say which kind of claim is being made whenever the small corpus is used as evidence.
context: LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project.
why: The same trap appeared twice on one project from opposite directions: a 39-record corpus that could not support any performance claim, and a ranking technique evaluated with a neighbourhood parameter of 10 against 45 items, which computes a penalty across roughly a fifth of the entire set and is nothing like the same parameter against thousands. The second was correctly flagged as untransferable rather than adopted, which is what makes the distinction worth stating explicitly rather than trusting to judgement.

content: **An abnormal outcome returned in the shape of a normal one gets acted on as success: give every distinct outcome a distinct shape.** An empty list that means both *nothing there* and *couldn't tell*, a write reported done at the wrong path, a record stored without a part it needed and no warning, an error variant swallowed by a catch-all match arm — each is byte-identical to the normal case, so the caller has nothing to branch on. The fix is structural: an enum variant with no wildcard arm, or a note that names what happened, so the difference survives to the caller. Where refusing would cost more than it saves, *report* is the same fix. Twelve of Scatterhoard's first 104 issues, 2026-08-01 to 2026-09-23.
context: Writing general forms for the four of Scatterhoard's nine common defect causes that had none, after re-deriving them over its 104 issues; same stretch as calibrating both shared sets and clearing the build directory.
why: Graduated from Scatterhoard's common-causes analysis, where it surfaced across the 95 issues filed after the original nine. It is distinct from the existing lesson that absence of a failure signal is not evidence of success: that one is about a check that never ran, this one about an outcome that ran and was misreported by its shape. It holds in any language — the mechanism is a return type too coarse to carry the difference — and catch-all arms are how a type that is fine-grained enough still loses it.

content: A test helper that loops until a condition clears must carry a bound and fail loudly when it is exceeded, never an unbounded loop. Under mutation testing, the mutation that removes the condition turns the helper into an infinite loop: bounded, it fails in seconds and names the tests that caught it; unbounded, the best available answer is a timeout that names nothing, and the pass pays the whole timeout budget to learn less. Found 2026-08-18 in paged-recall helpers that paged until a page came back empty.
context: Original found 2026-08-18 on Scatterhoard; the misattribution corrected 2026-08-26 after the same shape recurred deliberately and was traced to the runner. Checkable in that project's scripts/mutate.py at `run`.
why: Supersedes the original, which said the runner "reports nothing at all rather than reporting a caught mutation" and cited a four-hour wedged pass. Both were true of that runner and neither was true of unbounded helpers: the supervisor killed the test command without killing the test binary that held its output pipe, so the timeout could not fire at all — see [[01M10A5NDHE3GTDG8DHCQM9BRC]], found and fixed 2026-08-26. With the supervisor repaired, an unbounded helper costs a timeout rather than a wedged pass, which is a real cost and a smaller one. Worth correcting rather than deleting, because the advice survives its stated reason: naming the tests that caught a mutation is the whole output of a pass, and a timeout is the one outcome that names none.

content: To conclude a guard is missing, the probe must take the path a real caller takes. Calling a lower-layer function directly will always show the unguarded primitive -- that is what the layer above it is for -- so a probe that reaches past the guard proves nothing about whether the guard exists. Before filing an absence, search for the behaviour by name rather than for the mechanism: a grep for the error type found nothing, while the test that covered it was named for what it prevents.
context: Found 2026-08-23 on Scatterhoard, withdrawing the defect the same day it was filed. The withdrawn entry is kept in that project's ISSUES.md rather than deleted, because the mistake was more instructive than the entry.
why: This produced a wrongly filed high-severity defect that was recommended as the next work: a file carrying a duplicate identifier was said to import silently and lose a record, when the reader had always refused it and had both a test and a mutation. The probe had built the in-memory structure by hand and handed it to the storage call, bypassing the reader entirely. The failure is attractive because the probe *does* reproduce data loss -- the primitive really is unguarded -- so the evidence looks direct rather than misleading. Three separate false findings in one session came from badly built probes, the others being a Unicode test using two characters that were not a case pair and an end-to-end assertion that rode on a ranking cut rather than on the mechanism under test, so the cost is not hypothetical. Cheapest defences: name the real entry point before probing, and check that the probe fails for the reason claimed rather than merely fails.

content: When a paged result has to leave some items out, filter inside a bounded fetch loop, not after the page has been cut. Fetch a batch in rank order, drop what is excluded before loading anything expensive, and fetch again only if the page is not yet full. Filtering after a cut returns short pages, and a short page reads as the end. Over-fetching by the number excluded papers over that, but it grows with how far the caller has paged, and it loads exactly the items it throws away, because what a caller already holds is the top of the ranking. Where several sources are merged, the same shape is a merge that takes the best head one item at a time and stops at the limit. Pagination by continuing from the last key read keeps each batch from re-reading the ones before it.
context: Fixing a paging parameter ignored on one search path; the human partner asked for the fetch-filter-repeat loop in place of an over-fetch.
why: The over-fetch looked like a fix and passed every test, because tests check which items come back, not what was loaded to find them. A reviewer asking whether the function pulled everything into memory before truncating is what exposed it. The loop shape removes the question rather than tuning it, and it bounds memory by the batch size instead of by the match count.

content: When a change lets an operation create the state it reads — an identity, a key, a record — reread that state after the operation instead of reusing the value read before it. The earlier read was correct when written, because nothing downstream could create the value; the change made it silently stale. Search for every read of the newly creatable state that precedes an operation now able to create it.
context: Building Scatterhoard's set-settled-at-first-write in steps: create stopped minting a set's identity, the first write mints it, and minting an author became a new set's usual first write.
why: Observed twice on 2026-09-28 in Scatterhoard, in two functions changed by one decision. A set's identity moved from being minted at creation to being minted by its first write. Then `author_for` and, in a later step, `mint_author` each read the identity before a write that now created it, keyed a durable map row on that read, and so skipped the row whenever the write was the set's first. Nothing failed at the time; the loss showed only when a copy of the set was re-added and asked who the user was again. The second was found only because the first had been, by reading for the same shape. Two instances in one codebase; generalised because the mechanism is ordering alone.

content: Correctness of parts does not compose into usefulness of the whole. Tests written per layer verify that a layer keeps its promises; they cannot verify that the promises add up to a working product. When a layer is added above existing ones, re-read the design claims describing end-to-end behaviour and check each against what the new layer actually exposes — and exercise the real interface, because this class of defect is found by use rather than by the suite.
context: LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project, where the pattern recurred often enough to be named and counted.
why: A store held graph links, the domain type carried them, the file format round-tripped them, and every layer was tested and green. The client-facing surface never returned them, so the graph was invisible to the only client that existed — while a design document confidently described the graph as self-documenting because a caller could walk a returned record's links. That claim was false from the moment the surface was written. On that project twelve issues were found by driving the interface and none by the suite, which stopped being a run of bad luck and became the verification method.

content: **A deletion that leaves no trace can't be told apart from something that never existed, so everything that meets the gap misreads it: make a deletion a record.** In a system that merges, syncs, caches or indexes, a missing row is the most ambiguous signal there is. An older copy can bring the deleted item back as though it were new, an index keeps serving it, and a cascade removes the evidence that something downstream is now stale. The fix is a tombstone that carries what a later reader needs, such as the record's identity, its ancestry and the checksum it replaced, and to treat absence as meaning nothing at all. Five of Scatterhoard's first 104 issues, 2026-08-01 to 2026-09-23.
context: Writing general forms for the four of Scatterhoard's nine common defect causes that had none, after re-deriving them over its 104 issues; same stretch as calibrating both shared sets and clearing the build directory.
why: Graduated from Scatterhoard's common-causes analysis, where all five instances came from its tombstone work between 2026-08-07 and 2026-08-30. It holds for any system with more than one copy of its data or any derived structure over it, and the failure is quiet by construction — nothing fails on meeting an absence.

content: When a change adds or removes a side effect in an operation tests use as setup — a constructor, a create call, a fixture — run the full mutation pass, not only the mutations for the code you changed. A test that took its precondition from that setup keeps passing, now vacuously, and only the mutation of some unrelated guard it was protecting shows it.
context: Building Scatterhoard's set-settled-at-first-write steps 1 and 2 — create stops minting, then a shared set's first memory must be its charter — and reading a full mutation pass after each.
why: Observed twice on 2026-09-28 in Scatterhoard, once in each direction. First `create` stopped minting a set identity, and three tests that relied on the minted identity without saying so went vacuous. Then every fixture set gained a charter written at setup, and a test whose premise was an export taken while the set was still empty lost it: the charter write put an author record into that file, the path it existed to reach was never taken, and the suite stayed green. Both times only a full pass showed it. Superseded because the first version named only removal, and the second instance is the reverse change with the same effect. Two instances from one day's work in one codebase; generalised because the mechanism depends only on tests borrowing a precondition from shared setup.

content: When production runs with several of something and every test fixture has one, a whole class of defect is invisible to a green suite: anything about how the many are combined. Two defects in one function went unnoticed for months this way -- a per-item limit that was never summed, and a concatenation that was never ranked -- because both are identities when the count is one. Check the arity of each fixture against the real deployment, and write at least one test at the plural.
context: Found 2026-08-19 on Scatterhoard, where keyword search across memory sets applied its limit per set and concatenated the results unranked. Both halves became reachable only when a second set first existed on a real machine.
why: The single-instance fixture is the natural one to write: it is the smallest thing that exercises the feature, and it stays correct forever, so nothing ever prompts revisiting it. What makes this worth stating as a rule is that no amount of *additional* single-instance testing finds the defect -- coverage tools report the merge code as covered, because it runs; it simply cannot misbehave with one input. The signal to watch for is a configuration change that makes the plural case real for the first time, which is when these defects start being reachable in production while the suite stays green.

content: **Best-of-several-runs buys stability only when each run is itself stable.** Restarting a randomised search and keeping the best result is the obvious fix for an unstable answer, but if every run's draws move when the input changes, the candidates move too, and choosing the best among near-equal answers flips between them — measured worse than a single run. Make each run insertion-stable first (draws keyed to each item, not to position in a shared stream); then restarts converge on one winner and help. Measure the candidate fixes against the instability itself before choosing one.
context: Fixing unstable cluster descriptions in Scatterhoard, then building its charter-language declaration and one-live-charter guard, in one long session.
why: Measured 2026-09-14 on Scatterhoard's set description, with one memory removed at eight positions: with positional seeding, ten restarts lowered agreement with the whole-set partition on one set (adjusted Rand 0.61 to 0.45) and halved it on the other (0.88 to 0.46); with seeds keyed to memory ids, ten restarts raised the worst case to 0.95 and 0.98. The restart was the fix most sessions would reach for first. This extends the fixed-seed lesson it links to, which covers why positional draws are unstable but not what that does to restarts.

content: Instruction text has two failure classes with opposite feedback times, and treating them as one hides the cheap check. Behavioural drift -- how a rule actually gets applied -- is longitudinal and takes several sessions to see. Structural defects are not: they surface the first time anyone performs what the text describes, and reading cannot find them, including by the author minutes after writing. Three in one session, all in text drafted hours earlier: a rule that described a mechanism in the passive voice so nothing told anyone to perform it; a marker term that was also the name of the mechanism, so the list it produced was mostly memories about itself; and a length rule violated fourfold by its own author, because complying meant measuring something only the machine could see. So execute a new rule once, immediately, before believing it -- separately from living with it, which answers a different question later.
context: Drafting a convention across an evening, then exercising it once and finding three defects in it, having just argued that feedback on convention text is several sessions away.
why: The longitudinal claim is true and, read alone, it licenses waiting -- if the feedback is several sessions away, exercising it now looks pointless. It is not: the two classes have different instruments, and the structural one costs a single execution. What makes these three invisible to review is that each reads correctly. A passive sentence describing an effect looks like a rule; a marker named after its mechanism looks like good naming; a length rule looks followable until you try to follow it. Reviewing is reading, and reading is what already passed. The tell for the third one generalises: ask what the reader must measure to know they complied and where that measurement lives.

content: How a project adopts `coding-lessons`: a guide in six parts, each carrying this keyword and opening with its number. A project that adopts this set does two things with it. It keeps a few signposts for the lessons it is breaking most often now, and it recalls before writing, so every lesson has a chance to surface at the moment its mistake would be made. Both depend on triggers: memories describing the activity just before a mistake, each linked to the lesson it guards. The parts: 1, the opt-in sentence; 2, recall before writing; 3, record a failure; 4, choose signposts; 5, write a trigger; 6, record what the habit catches. A session follows this guide only where its project's `AGENTS.md` says to, and the numbers in it are defaults a project may change with prompting of its own.
context: Writing this set's adoption guide from the decisions made while designing how projects use it, reviewed by the human partner before export.
why: The overview of a guide split across memories, because no one memory can hold it. The parts carry their numbers in their text because keyword recall orders by id, and superseding a part gives it a later one.

content: A refusal that names an alternative gets read as a price on the plan you already had, not as a reason to re-derive the goal. The intent is formed before the tool speaks, so the cheapest response is to evaluate the named substitute against that intent -- and where the substitute costs more, the honest-looking conclusion is to do nothing, which is also the conclusion that requires no work. Treat a refusal as the moment to restate what you were trying to achieve, before pricing anything: ask what you know now that made you want the change, rather than whether the offered instrument is worth it.
context: Found 2026-08-30 on Scatterhoard. A memory's confidence was to be raised because its prediction had just come true; the new service gate refused the amendment and named supersession; the supersession was priced as "a second copy of an unchanged claim for a 0.05 move" and dropped -- when what had actually happened was that new evidence existed and belonged in the memory's content. The human partner asked why, which is how it surfaced.
why: Refusals arrive after planning, which is what makes this reliable rather than occasional -- the substitute is compared against a goal that has already been narrowed to one operation. The direction of the error is not random either: abandoning is free, so the reasoning that ends in no action is the one that feels efficient, and it can be perfectly sound about the question it answers while answering the wrong question. The tell is a refusal met with a defensible-sounding argument for doing nothing at all; a goal genuinely worth an operation is usually worth some other operation.

content: A tool's per-field description is load-bearing instruction text, and what it produces is measurable in the data the tool collects. Measured across two memory corpora: a field described in one line, and marked optional, was filled on 98% of records — and the contents came back as the description's own vocabulary. It opened with "when", and 89% of the values carried a date that another field already held; it said "not searched", and 72% carried reference material parked there because the phrase read as licence. Before adding guidance about how to fill a field, read what the current description has already produced; the drift is usually the description being obeyed, not ignored.
context: Rewriting the description of a free-text field on a memory tool, after measuring what its previous wording had produced across two live corpora. Working out whether guidance of that kind belongs beside the field or in a separately served instruction set.
why: The instinct on finding badly-filled fields is to add guidance somewhere authoritative — a style guide, a served instruction, a review rule — which treats the existing description as inert. The measurement says the opposite: compliance was near-total, including with the parts nobody meant as instructions. That makes the description the cheapest and highest-leverage place to intervene, and it makes the field's contents a usable instrument for testing wording, since what comes back is the wording's own effect. It also inverts the usual worry: the risk is not that a description will be ignored, it is that an offhand clause will be followed exactly.

content: A reduced projection silently disables every rule that reads the fields it drops. Adding a summary or index mode is normally judged on cost, but it also changes what a reader can *evaluate*: a rule of the form "a result carrying only X is not really a Y", and any ranking the reader is supposed to notice, both need fields the projection removes. Nothing fails when this happens -- the rules are usually prose in documentation or instructions rather than code, so no type checks them and no test covers them. When you add a projection, list what the callers of that path were told to do with the full response, and check each instruction against what the projection actually carries.
context: Writing the convention text for a session-start index, the morning after building the index projection itself.
why: Met while writing an instruction and its filtering rule for a recall that had just been given an index mode: the rule said to look at a hit's keywords, and an index hit is an id and one line. The rule and the mode were designed hours apart by the same session, and the collision was invisible from either end -- the mode's design listed what it omits and the rule's design named what it reads, and nobody put the two lists side by side. The repair is cheap when caught here and expensive later, because the rule keeps looking correct: it describes a check a reader cannot perform, so it fails as *nothing happening* rather than as an error. The general remedy is to move such a filter to the query, where it acts on what the caller sends rather than on what the response shows.

content:
When a test needs a helper that reaches past the public interface to build a state that interface is supposed to be able to reach, treat the helper as a defect report rather than as setup. It converts a failing test into a passing one: the feature is then proven to work *from a state the product cannot get to*, which is not the claim anyone wanted.

The tell is specific enough to check for — a helper writing directly to storage, or otherwise going around the API, to manufacture a precondition the API itself is meant to produce. Fixture builders that assemble *inputs* are ordinary; ones that assemble *the system's own state* are worth a second look.
context: The helper was `forget_the_set_identity`, deleting a row from a store's `meta` before an import; it and its call are gone now that adoption refuses only an identity the set has written under. Recorded in that project's ISSUES.md as `a-re-added-set-cannot-recover-its-identity`.
why:
Found 2026-09-02 on Scatterhoard. A set could not adopt the identity carried in a file it imported, because creating the set minted one first and adoption refused to displace it — so the sanctioned way to take on an existing set silently dropped its identity. The suite had a test asserting adoption works, and it passed, because a helper deleted the minted identity by hand beforehand. That helper *was* the defect, written down as a fixture and running green for weeks.

What makes this worth a rule rather than a one-off: the helper reads as diligence. It has a descriptive name, it does exactly what it says, and the test around it genuinely exercises the code path — from a starting state no user can produce. Nothing in a green suite distinguishes that from a legitimate fixture, and a mutation corpus cannot help either, since the guard is real and the test does reach it. Removing the helper is the whole diagnosis: if the test then fails, the product cannot do what the test claimed.

content: A test that constructs the request itself does not test what a client can reach. Where a published schema stands between the caller and the code -- an MCP tool definition, an OpenAPI spec, a GraphQL schema, a form -- a validating client drops fields the schema does not declare, so a guard against a field the schema omits is unreachable no matter how well the handler is written and tested. Check that the schema admits the input, not only that the handler rejects it.
context: Found 2026-08-21 in Scatterhoard, attempting from a client the thing a smoke-test item described. `hoard_correct`'s amend refuses `content` and `why` with a message naming supersession; neither is in the tool's published schema, so the client stripped them and the server answered a different refusal. Checkable as `amending-a-claim-is-refused-where-no-client-can-reach-it` in that project's ISSUES.md.
why: The suite stays green in the most convincing way there is: the guard exists, a test exercises it, and the assertion is about the right thing. What is missing is a step the test skipped rather than one it got wrong, so nothing about the test looks suspicious. Worth checking whenever a refusal is written for a caller's likely mistake, because a refusal is exactly the case where the field is one the schema had no reason to declare.

content: **A fact written down twice and kept in step by hand will drift, and silently: derive the copy, or delete it.** Each copy stays internally consistent, so nothing fails — a hand-written schema beside the types it describes, prose describing a function beside the function, a second code path applying the same rule, a test's hard-coded anchor into source text. Where a copy genuinely must exist, make a check compare it against its source rather than against a literal, so drift becomes a failure. The most common single cause of defects in Scatterhoard's first 104 issues, 2026-08-01 to 2026-09-23.
context: Re-deriving Scatterhoard's common causes of defects across its 104 issues, and moving the analysis out of a hand-written section of its tracking file.
why: Graduated from Scatterhoard's common-causes analysis on 2026-09-23, where it had been cause #1 since the first nine issues and was the one of the three original causes never carried into this set. It holds on any codebase in any language — the mechanism is duplication kept in step by attention, which fails the same way everywhere — and the fix is structural rather than a call for care, which is what makes it worth a lesson.

content: **Code written as though one process holds the data breaks when a second arrives: name the state each process keeps privately, and key its invalidation to the shared state.** Any in-memory cache, any setting chosen per process, any build that replaces a binary other processes are running is a private copy of shared state. It stays correct only while nothing else writes. Examples: a database opened in a locking mode that lets one writer shut out every reader, a cache nothing invalidates when another process writes, two processes that disagree about a setting and redo each other's work. The fix is an invalidation signal the store itself provides (SQLite's `PRAGMA data_version`, WAL with a busy timeout), and reads that never rebuild. Publishing or syncing extends the same cause from processes to machines. Five of Scatterhoard's first 104 issues, 2026-08-01 to 2026-09-23.
context: Writing general forms for the four of Scatterhoard's nine common defect causes that had none, after re-deriving them over its 104 issues; same stretch as calibrating both shared sets and clearing the build directory.
why: Graduated from Scatterhoard's common-causes analysis. It holds for any system whose storage outlives one process, which is most of them — and the single-process assumption is invisible in development because development usually runs one process. The machine-level extension is why a breaking change is cheap only before the first copy leaves the machine.

content: 3. Record a failure: record each mistake a lesson here describes as an instance of it, in the project's own set. Link the record `instance_of` to the lesson, and say what went wrong, where, and when. The record is the project's, so it uses the project's nouns, and the link is cross-set, naming `coding-lessons`. Where no lesson fits and the mistake would recur on a different codebase, write the lesson here first; if it would not, it is the project's alone. These records are what signposts are chosen from, and nothing keeps a count: the count is the number of these links.
context: Writing this set's adoption guide from the decisions made while designing how projects use it, reviewed by the human partner before export.
why: A count kept by hand drifts from what it counts; a derived one cannot. The routing when no lesson fits is this set's charter applied to a failure.

content: When a guard filters on how something is written rather than on what it is, ask what happens when it is written the other way. A defence against a hostile cross-boundary reference keyed on the presence of a qualifier field, so an attacker who omitted the qualifier and wrote a bare identifier bypassed it entirely -- and the bare form was the easier thing to hand-write, so the repair defended the harder attack and left the obvious one open. The re-keyed guard asks who holds the thing being pointed at, which is a fact about the data rather than about its spelling, and cannot be spelled around.
context: Found 2026-08-23 on Scatterhoard, a day after the original repair was committed and believed complete. Found by tracing whether a proposed feature could re-open the defect, not by any test aimed at it.
why: A spelling filter looks like a defence and tests like one, because the test is written from the same mental model as the guard: whoever imagined the attack imagined it in the form they defended against. That makes it invisible to review, since reviewer and author share the model. The cheap check is to enumerate the ways one relationship can be expressed and confirm the guard catches each, done at the moment the guard is written -- afterwards its existence is itself the reason nobody looks. The shape generalises past security: any rule keyed on surface form has this exposure, which is why canonicalising at the boundary and keying the rule on the canonical form is the more durable arrangement.

content:
**An environment obstacle does not feel like a moment for recall, so stored knowledge about the environment goes unused.** Guidance to search memory before acting tends to be written with decisions in mind — a design choice, something the human called settled, work that may have been done before. A missing tool is none of those. It presents as a mechanical problem with an obvious next move, so the session starts solving instead of asking, and never classifies the moment as one the rule covers.

The instance: a session needed text out of a PDF, found no extractor, wrote its own parser, got nothing, and asked the human partner to install a package — which failed for an unrelated reason and cost them a detour. A memory written six days earlier, in the same store, named the absent tooling and the built-in method that works. It was never recalled, because at no point did extracting a PDF feel like a question the project might already have answered.

**The check is cheap and the trigger is easy to state: when the environment blocks you, search before you work around it.** Anything you are about to ask a human to install is the strongest form of that signal — an install request leaves the session, spends someone else's attention, and can fail for reasons neither of you can see. Environment facts are also exactly the kind that accumulate in a personal store rather than in a repository, so they are invisible to a glance at the code and recoverable only by asking.
context: Trying to read a PDF during a design session, and discovering afterwards that the working method had been written down six days earlier.
why:
Recorded because the instance is clean and the cost was paid by someone else. Asking a human to install software is a request that leaves the session and occupies them; here it sent them into an unrelated failure, for a problem already solved.

The reason it is worth a memory rather than being covered by the existing rule is that the rule names the wrong moments. Guidance about recalling first is written with design decisions in mind, and the session that skips it is not disobeying — it never classified what it was doing as a decision at all.

At 0.8 rather than higher because it generalises from a single clean instance; the mechanism is plain, but whether environment obstacles are the *main* blind spot or just one of several is not something one case can settle.

content: **A batch call that returns one result for the whole batch lets one bad item fail every item in it — and a retrying sweep over pending work turns that into a permanent stall.** The shape: `fn process(items) -> Result<Vec<Output>, Error>`, built by collecting per-item results with `?`, plus a background pass that sends every pending item through one call. An item that can never succeed now fails the batch on every pass, so nothing pending is ever processed, and whatever waits on the pass fails with it. The error names no item, because the batch had no way to say which. **Return an outcome per item** — `Result<Vec<Outcome>, Error>`, where the outer error means the tool itself is broken and a per-item variant means *this item has no answer*. Keep a strict all-or-nothing wrapper for callers that really want one, and make sure the retrying path never calls it.
context: Fixing a store-stopping failure in Scatterhoard's embedding path, where one memory the model could not represent blocked a whole store. Same stretch: deciding how a sweep should record a permanent no-result, and whether the sweep should run on writes at all.
why:
A batch boundary is also a failure boundary, and it stays invisible until an item arrives that fails *every* time: transient failures clear on the next retry and hide the shape completely. So a design that has only ever met transient failures has never tested this.

Evidence, kept with its project: in the scatterhoard memory store (2026-09-11), an embedding call collected per-text vector construction into one result, and the gap sweep embedded every unembedded record through one call. One record in a script the model had no tokens for stopped every later write to its store and every semantic search across all stores. Recorded there as `one-unembeddable-memory-stops-the-store`.

content: When a recorded mutation survives, run it against the whole suite before concluding a test is missing. A mutation runner that runs only the test binaries named for each mutation reports *survives* whenever the covering test lives outside that list, and the diagnosis that follows — write a new test — duplicates coverage that already exists while leaving the routing that hid it in place. Trigger: about to write a test to catch a surviving mutation.
context: Fixing Scatterhoard's reembed-count mutation, right after recalibrating the recall floors on two sets.
why: Observed 2026-09-30 in Scatterhoard: a mutation recorded `caught` survived, and its issue prescribed a new test with a memory the model cannot represent. That test had already existed, in `tests/unrepresentable.rs`, the whole time; the mutation named only `tests/sets.rs`. Adding the binary to its list caught it at once. One instance, so the generalisation is inferred rather than established, and it applies only to runners that select tests per mutation.

content: Every scalar crossing an interface should say what it describes and what it is relative to — in the field name where possible, in the payload otherwise. If neither can be arranged, do not send the number. A caller cannot recover a missing referent by inspection and will supply the obvious wrong one instead. Being alone in a payload is not the same as being unambiguous.
context: LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project, where three of the five are still open issues.
why: Five single numbers on one tool surface were each correct arithmetic reported so as to invite a wrong reading: a similarity describing one memory while sitting beside another's content, a budget a caller could not tell was a bound or a target, a 0.0 whose baseline was the only item in the store. A wrong reading of a number leaves no trace, which is why these cost nothing visible and were still worth fixing.

content: **When you change what output is sorted by, run every snapshot of that output several times, not once.** If the old key matched the order fixtures are created in — time-ordered ids, auto-increment keys — the snapshots were deterministic only by that accident. A new key that depends on random data leaves them passing sometimes, and one green run proves nothing.
context: Changing Scatterhoard's memory-file order to reduce merge conflicts, and finding an approval test that had been stable by coincidence.
why: Observed 2026-09-21 on Scatterhoard. Moving the exported memory file from id order to a hash of each id made an approval snapshot of an exported file fail ten runs in twelve: its ids are minted fresh each run, and under id order mint order had always been file order. It passed on the run that re-recorded it. The fix was to sort inside the recording, since that snapshot is about the shape of each line, and to assert the order separately with chosen ids. Evidence in the `scatterhoard` set under `concurrent-additions-collide-at-the-end-of-the-memory-file`. One instance.

content: Before marking a design question resolved, walk one concrete scenario end to end — actual values, an actual sequence of events, and an actual adversary where relevant. If the resolution cannot be walked, it is not finished.
context: LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project. Cheap compared with the alternative, which is discovering it after code depends on it.
why: Three separately-resolved decisions turned out to have holes, all found within hours and all by the same move of asking what happens in a specific situation: a type written without a field that a cross-reference had been defined to include weeks earlier, a derivation specified as happening "at load time" when the thing it derived changes on write, and a file header trusted as authoritative, which made it a privilege-escalation channel. None was caught by re-reading the prose, which had been reviewed several times.

content: **In Rust, doc comments for several items can silently merge into one, and the compiler reports nothing.** Consecutive `///` lines with no item between them are a single doc comment attached to the *next* item, so if an item is deleted or moved out from under its documentation, that documentation does not become orphaned — it joins the block below it. Nothing warns: a doc comment with no item at all is an error, but a doc comment with too much in it is valid. Found 2026-09-15 in a 6,900-line Rust file where four functions' doc blocks had stacked onto one function over time; three public functions were left with no documentation of their own, and their text — including `# Errors` sections — was rendering under a fourth function's name. **The detection that works is structural, not visual**: list the items in a region and check each one has its own block, because reading the file top to bottom shows a long, plausible comment and the eye supplies the missing boundary. The same shape exists wherever comments attach to the following item rather than being delimited.
context: Clearing two long-standing tidy-ups in Scatterhoard while building command-line export; one of them was a doc comment said to be sitting above the wrong function, which turned out to be four blocks glued together.
why:
Recorded because every safeguard that would normally catch it does not. The code compiles, the tests pass, `clippy` is silent, and `rustfmt` reformats around it without comment — and the rendered documentation looks *complete*, because the merged text is real documentation, just filed under the wrong name. The only signals are absence, which nothing reports, and misplacement, which requires reading two screens of prose to notice.

Worth the entry rather than being obvious from the language rules: the rule is well known, and the failure it produces is not, because the thing that goes missing is documentation for items nobody is looking at. A missing `# Errors` section on a public function is also the kind of thing a lint *would* catch if the block were absent rather than misattached, which is what makes this the quiet variant.

Not generalised beyond languages whose comments attach to a following item; in a language with delimited doc blocks the same edit leaves a stray block instead, which is visible.

content: A rule that governs a reflexive action cannot live in retrieved memory. Searching is itself a deliberate act, so a rule reachable only by recall arrives after any action taken without deliberation -- reaching for a familiar tool, applying a default format, taking the usual route. The rules with this shape are recognisable in advance: they say *not that way* about something done by habit rather than by decision. Put those in whatever context arrives unconditionally at the start of every session, and leave retrieval to serve the rules whose moment already involves a pause.
context: Found 2026-08-26 on Scatterhoard, on putting a decision to the human partner as a multiple-choice prompt with a confidence-1.0 memory saying not to. The repair was to move the rule into always-loaded context rather than to try harder at recalling it.
why: A preference stated once, recorded at the highest confidence there is, and available to the session that broke it -- broken anyway, because the moment it governed did not feel like one worth searching about. The nearest recorded lesson answers a different question: it says put a constraint where the work is, so it is reachable without knowing to look, and its example is a notice carried by every file. That fixes reachability at the work site, and there is no site here -- what fails is timing rather than location, and the failure is silent because a rule not consulted looks exactly like a rule with nothing to say. The practical test is whether you would think to search at the moment the rule applies; if the honest answer is no, the storage medium has already decided the outcome.

content: Collecting: questions asked during review that reliably turn up defects. A case fits when the question asked for a fact that was cheap to check and was being carried as an assumption -- often about a boundary, and never asking for an opinion. Members carry `defect-finding`; the cases so far are in the memory this points at. Ends when the shapes reduce to a way of generating new questions, or when twenty cases have failed to reduce them.
context: Landing the watch convention and putting the first memory on the session-start list. The same evening had rewritten the context field's description, retired the recall-gloss convention, and found that nothing in the catalog actually asked anyone to do the session-start recall.
why: Made active 2026-09-04, as the first `hoard-watch` memory. It is the purest push case available: nobody would ever search for *what shape was that question*, so no query reaches this collection and it can only arrive unprompted. The ending is stated because marking obliges it, and it is stated as a count as well as a condition because a collection of confirming cases cannot judge its own saturation -- twenty is a bound that can be checked by someone who was not there, where "when it stops being useful" cannot. It is a separate memory from the seed it points at rather than a rewrite of it: the seed's own reasoning is that the distribution of cases is the finding and rewriting collapses it, so the six gathered cases stay where they were recorded and this carries only what has to be short enough to push.

content: When records are shipped into a context window, measure the per-record envelope before assuming that writing shorter will control the cost. Below a certain payload size the envelope dominates and the cost stops responding to the prose: measured on one memory tool, identifiers, two timestamps, attribution and field names came to 411 characters that do not shrink, so a 350-character payload was 46% envelope and cutting the payload to 150 barely moved the total. Past that point the lever is a projection -- ship a derived line and fetch the record on demand -- not discipline about length.
context: Probing whether a session-start push list survives a realistic number of entries, after an evening spent designing one. The same stretch had rewritten a field description on the same tool and retired a convention.
why: "Write shorter" is the available instruction and it feels like the responsible one, so a design reaches for it and then holds the line badly for years. The arithmetic says it cannot work: at a hundred records the difference between a terse payload and a generous one was 3.1x versus 4.2x the same reference budget, where a derived index line was 0.4x. What makes this worth stating as a rule is that the envelope is invisible at the point of authoring -- the author sees prose and the transport carries a record -- so nobody notices which term dominates until it is measured. The projection also removes the failure mode rather than guarding it: once only a derived line ships, an over-long record costs the same as a short one and the length rule can be dropped instead of enforced.

content: Examples placed inside a rule narrow it by implication. A reader anchors on the concrete list and treats it as the set of things the rule covers, so whatever the list omits quietly stops counting — even when the rule's own general clause plainly admits it. Put the criterion in the rule and the examples somewhere subordinate to it, or leave them out. When a case turns out to be missing, the repair is to cut the list rather than extend it: adding items chases one category at a time, and a list can only ever hold the categories somebody already thought of.
context: Found 2026-08-24 on Scatterhoard, cutting the enumeration from its `store-when` convention and adding guidance that a memory set's charter must describe its subject rather than list the kinds of record it takes.
why: Measured on Scatterhoard's memory conventions 2026-08-24. A rule saying to record anything a later session would spend real effort working out again was followed with five examples, all of them kinds of *conclusion*; a measurement procedure devised during a session went unrecorded, and was noticed only because the human partner asked for it by name. The same shape appeared one layer down in the descriptions each memory set gives of itself, where the set whose description named technique accumulated technique and the set whose description named four kinds of conclusion did not — same governing rule over both, opposite corpora. The tempting fix in both places was a sixth item, which would have deepened the effect it was meant to repair.

content: Give an LLM-assisted project a short vision document that the LLM may not modify without the human partner's explicit approval, and require every design decision to conform to it. It works as an anchor because it is small enough to load in full, states intent rather than mechanism, and changes only by a human act — so a long series of individually reasonable steps has something fixed to be checked against. Without one, drift is invisible from inside: each step is justified by the step before it, and nothing in the chain is wrong.
context: The practice is from the Scatterhoard project, whose vision document carries the constraint in its own text and states that maintainers will reject submissions deviating from it. Untested against a case where the vision itself was wrong and needed to change under pressure.
why: The failure mode this addresses is not an LLM proposing something bad, but a project ratcheting away from its purpose through changes that are each defensible. A design document can be revised to accommodate whatever was just decided, which quietly makes it a record of decisions rather than a constraint on them. Withholding write access from the party doing most of the writing is what keeps the document upstream of the work instead of downstream of it.

content: A fallback chain that resolves several sources into a single value discards which source answered, and any later policy needing to treat them differently has nowhere to look. Where the sources differ in *authority* -- something a person deliberately configured, versus something the environment supplied -- carry the provenance alongside the value, or resolve at the point of use rather than at startup. The cost of the collapse is not a wrong default; it is that a wrong default can no longer be distinguished from a right one.
context: `whoami()` in src/main.rs and its path through `author_or_claim`; the Scatterhoard-specific consequences are in documents/design/memory-data-model.md under the attribution proposal.
why: Found 2026-08-31 on Scatterhoard: `whoami()` resolves `SCATTERHOARD_AUTHOR`, then `$USER`, then a literal, into one String at startup. That was adequate until a design needed to ask whether a name had been *chosen* by the person or *supplied* by the operating system -- a question the resolved value could no longer answer, though every input to it could. The consequence was already sitting in the data: 155 records attributed to a macOS account name, with no way for code to tell that attribution apart from a deliberate one, so no rule could be written to refuse the first and accept the second. Collapse is attractive because it simplifies every consumer, and the loss stays invisible until some consumer needs the distinction -- which may be long after the resolution code is settled and trusted.

content: **When an artifact lives in the repository and its activation lives in per-clone configuration, the two fail independently — and testing the artifact tells you nothing about whether anyone is running it.** Git merge drivers, hooks, clean/smudge filters, editor settings, opt-in CI steps: the thing is committed, the switch that turns it on is not, so every collaborator must enable it and nothing reminds them. The failure is quiet in the worst direction — a driver that merges perfectly and is registered nowhere produces exactly the conflicts it exists to prevent, **while looking installed to whoever wrote it**, because their clone is the one where it works. So an item like this has two acceptance conditions, not one: the artifact behaves, and the unregistered case degrades **safely rather than quietly**. Track them separately, or the half that finishes first closes the item.
context: Migrating a project's backlog, where an entry insisted its registration risk be tracked in a separate file from its implementation.
why:
Recorded because the two look like one piece of work and inviting an obvious consolidation, and consolidating puts the activation risk inside an item whose done-condition is *the artifact is written* — which is always the half completed first.

Two instances from one project. A field-aware merge driver was designed with plain merge as the fallback, and its registration risk was deliberately filed in a different tracking file from its implementation, on the stated grounds that the driver working and the driver being registered have failed independently for other people. And the same project's own `PreCompact` hook ships as a committed script with **uncommitted** wiring, because the wiring carries an absolute path a collaborator cannot share — the identical shape, arrived at for an unrelated reason, and equally invisible to anyone whose machine already has it.

content: Signposts are withdrawn from this set's adoption guide as of 2026-10-04. The guide had a project keep up to three, for the lessons with the most instances among its last 20 recorded failures. Replayed against the first adopting project's 38 recorded failures, they would have been in place before 4. Of the rest, 27 were the first instance of their lesson, which no signpost can precede, and 7 were a lesson's second, which the two-instance minimum could not yet signpost. Signposting every lesson ever seen reached 11, and for a new adopter they start at zero. They may return as an experiment after the first release.
context: Revising this set's adoption for its first release to beta testers, after measuring that the habit faded and that signposts would rarely have preceded a failure.
why: Supersedes part 4 without the guide's keyword, so recalling the guide no longer returns it as a step, while the reason it went stays readable. No session on the first adopting project ever chose a signpost, so they were withdrawn on the replay's evidence, not on observed failure.

content: **Committing the primary record before a fallible derived step, then reporting the step's failure, leaves the record stored behind an error saying it was not.** The caller believes nothing happened. The record is there anyway, often with no id returned to find it by, and anything that later processes it meets the same failure. If the derived step is pure computation, **do it first**, and commit the record together with its derived data in one transaction — then an error means nothing was written. Getting the reporting right is not enough: the failure has to happen *before* the commit, not merely be reported after it. The general form covers any write followed by a fallible derivation — indexing, thumbnailing, validation after insert.
context: Fixing a store-stopping failure in Scatterhoard's embedding path, where a failed write was committed anyway. Same stretch: per-item embedding outcomes and a verdict row for text the model cannot represent.
why:
The trap is that each half looks correct on its own: the write succeeds and says nothing, the derivation fails and says so. Only their order makes the combined report false, and the caller is then left unable to repair what it was told does not exist.

Evidence, kept with its project: in the scatterhoard memory store (2026-09-11), a write committed the memory and then embedded it. When embedding failed, the tool returned an error with no id, the memory was stored anyway, and a sweep kept re-failing on it — so the only repair, deleting the memory, needed an id the caller never received. Recorded there as `one-unembeddable-memory-stops-the-store`.

content: A guard can want a fact that nearby state cannot honestly supply, and the fix is to remove the guard's dependency rather than to pick a collapse rule. A save-first rule was gated on a per-set dirty flag, but once reconciliation bases became per-record-and-target the flag had no single value. Both readings — dirty against any target, dirty against every target — over-read the base, which records a past agreement between two replicas and never claimed anything about what is on disk now. So the destructive operations now always write the safety copy, and read no state out of the database they are about to destroy.
context: Decided 2026-08-06 on the Scatterhoard project, recorded in documents/design/set-lifecycle.md under "Resolved: the save is unconditional, and no flag gates it". Moved here from the personal set 2026-08-15.
why: The question stood open across two sessions framed as "which collapse rule is right", and both candidates were defensible, which is what kept it stuck. It dissolved once the base was read for what it is: merge ancestry, not a saved-ness claim. The tell was that the safer reading made the gate pass in nearly every real configuration — a guard that does not discriminate is not a guard to tune.

content:
**A correlation across group means is not a correlation across members, and bucketed tables are where this gets in.** Grouping data into buckets and correlating the bucket averages inflates the apparent relationship, often enormously: the within-group scatter that would sink it has been averaged away before you look. The same data at member level can be uncorrelated, or correlated the other way. **The tell is that you are reading a table whose rows are categories.** Any table of the form *class, mean X, mean Y* is a group-mean correlation whether or not anyone computes r on it, and reading down the columns to see a trend is doing the arithmetic by eye.

**The discipline is to compute it per member before believing it**, which is nearly always cheap since the member-level data is what the means came from. When the two disagree, the member-level answer is the one about the mechanism; the group-level one is about how the groups were chosen. In one case seven class medians gave r 0.827 where the 202 underlying members gave −0.338 — a sign flip, and the groups had been defined by the author.
context: Refuting a fragmentation hypothesis that had looked strong across class medians, at the end of a long recall investigation.
why:
Learned three times in one investigation before being written down, which is the reason it is worth writing down. Each time the shape was identical: bucket the data by a suspected cause, read the means, see a clean monotone rise, and believe it. Each time the member-level correlation was near zero. Buckets defined by the person doing the analysis are especially dangerous, because the grouping variable is then chosen — knowingly or not — to separate the outcome.

The reason it keeps working is that a bucketed table looks like a summary rather than a claim. Nobody feels they are computing a correlation when they read five rows and notice the last column goes up, so no one applies the scepticism they would apply to an r. That is exactly what makes the tell — *rows are categories* — more useful than any statistical rule: it fires at reading time.

Confidence 0.85: this is textbook ecological fallacy rather than a discovery, but the specific failure mode — believing a bucketed table you built yourself, repeatedly, in one sitting — is the practical form it takes and is not what the textbook warns about.

content: A recorded mutation's find text must be anchored on something unique to the function under test. One mutation aimed at a keyword constructor used a line that was also the last line of a different constructor; the runner mutated the other one, that type's own test caught it, and the record read as proof about keywords. Anchor on something only the target has.
context: Found 2026-08-04 on the Scatterhoard project. A related hazard: a find keyed to a literal breaks silently when that literal legitimately moves. Moved here from the personal set 2026-08-15.
why: An ambiguous find is a silent mis-aim rather than an error — the runner has no way to notice it matched the wrong function, and the mutation reports as caught while proving nothing. This is the exact failure mode mutation testing exists to protect against, occurring inside the mutation record itself.

content: A rule for correcting a stale record does nothing unless something prompts you to notice it went stale, and the moment that matters is not when you write — it is when you *change the world the record describes*. That moment has no natural boundary: you were doing something else, the change succeeded, and nothing about it mentions the record. Where a system has a check that runs before writing, it will not fire here, because the failure case produces no write at all. Add the question to whatever boundary already fires reliably: what did I change today that something already recorded now describes wrongly?
context: Found 2026-08-24 on Scatterhoard, tracing a stale figure in its memory corpus back to the session that raised the value.
why: A configuration constant was raised, correctly, and documented in three places in the repository. A record elsewhere still stated the old value and nothing marked it stale, so for eleven days it answered confidently and wrongly, and the wrong answer was reached again by a later reader who checked the source of truth and stopped at the first heading that matched. The check that would have caught it ran only before storing something new, and nothing new was being stored — raising the constant produced no record, it invalidated one. That is the general shape: an invalidation is silent in a way an addition is not, because an addition passes through the machinery and an invalidation goes around it.

content: A rule about how artifacts get written can be evaluated by an observable in the artifacts themselves, measured before and after it took effect -- no instrumented run required, because the output is the record. Two moves make it sharper. **Replay counterfactually**: for each artifact, ask what the rule prescribes and whether following it at that moment would have changed the outcome, evaluated against the state as it stood then rather than now. And **decompose the failure**: where the prescribed step would have worked and was not taken, the rule was not followed; where it was taken and would not have worked, the mechanism it depends on is the problem. Those want different fixes, and a single adherence number hides which one you have.
context: Worked out 2026-08-30 on Scatterhoard, on the human partner's question of whether the effectiveness of its served conventions can be measured objectively. The precedent that suggested it was already in the project: one convention was written because someone measured a field's distribution and found it used across a fifth of its range.
why: The reflex is to conclude that a rule about judgement can only be judged, and then to argue about it. But a rule worth writing usually predicts something countable in what it governs -- a duplicate that should not exist, a field used across a fifth of its range, a name coined where one already existed. The counterfactual is what turns a count into evidence about the rule rather than about the work: raw counts move with how much was written and what it was about. Read the result with the confound stated rather than buried: a before-and-after across a ship date is objective without being controlled, and where the author of the rule is also its subject, "the rule worked" and "the author was thinking about it" cannot be separated at all.

content: Where a check can pass for several different reasons, the report must say which — because the weakest reason and the strongest look identical in a summary, and the weak one is the direction a corpus rots in. A mutation runner counted a mutation as caught if any test failed, if the tests hung, or if the crate failed to compile. All three are defensible, but only the first proves a test noticed: the third means the replacement text no longer makes sense, which happens on its own as the code it constructs gains fields. Seven of 243 records had rotted that way and every pass reported them as coverage. The fix is to name the mechanism in the summary and require the weak one to be declared per record, so an undeclared one is a disagreement rather than a pass.
context: Found 2026-08-26 on Scatterhoard after three such records were noticed by reading pass output by hand; adding the report found four more. Checkable in that project's scripts/mutate.py at `BY_THE_COMPILER`, and in scripts/mutations.py, where the third `expect` value is documented.
why: This is the layer beneath [[01M0XZW2FGFHS9ZZJ0KG0NE7VQ]], which established that only a full run reports outcomes and that a staleness check cannot see a record that stopped proving anything. Both hold here and neither was enough: the full runs *did* run, and printed the mechanism on each line, but the summary said "all N behaved as recorded" and that is the line anyone reads. So a check can be honest per item and misleading in aggregate. The reason it rots one way rather than both is worth keeping: a record that becomes uncompilable still reports as caught, while one that becomes uncatchable reports as a disagreement and gets fixed — so the failure mode is asymmetric, and it accumulates on the flattering side.

content: **On macOS, `pkill` and `pgrep` stop reading options at the first pattern, so an option written after it becomes another pattern.** `pkill -f "server$" -n` does not kill the newest match: `-n` is a second pattern, and with `-f` it matches any command line containing `-n`, which takes in most Electron and browser helpers (`--no-sandbox` and the like). One kill aimed at a single test server took down unrelated desktop applications. Put every option before the pattern; better, kill the PID you already have; and before any pattern kill, run the identical arguments through `pgrep -l` and read what they match. Never send a kill's stderr to `/dev/null`.
context: Starting the scatterhoard set's full export review, which timed out; timing review pages on a scratch copy of the store, debug build against release, and fixing a sort that reran the privacy pre-pass on every comparison.
why: Observed 2026-10-29: the command was meant for one throwaway server started from a scratch directory, and its PID was already known. The same arguments under `pgrep -l` afterwards listed ten processes across three applications, confirming the cause. GNU procps permutes arguments, so the same line works on Linux, which is what makes it look safe. Silenced stderr removed the last chance to notice. The cost falls on the person's other work rather than on the task, so the check has to come before the kill: afterwards there is nothing to undo.

content:
Effort has a floor it cannot push an error rate below, for humans and for models alike. Past that floor, further investment belongs in tooling, environment, process and recovery — a check that fires, a refusal, a safe default, a cheap undo — rather than in resolving to be more careful. Treat *try harder* as a plan only until the same mistake recurs under deliberate attention; after that it is evidence about the remedy, not about the person.

The corollary is what makes it usable: a remedy that does not lower the failure *rate* can still be the right one, if it lowers the *cost* of each failure. Those are different quantities and only the second is reliably purchasable.

Worth recording because the instinct runs the other way. A recurring slip feels like a discipline problem, and the honest-seeming response is to attend harder — which is unfalsifiable while it keeps failing quietly, and which crowds out the cheaper structural fix.
context: Scatterhoard, whose ISSUES.md entry `malformed-tool-call-damage-is-stored-silently` carries the occurrence record and now says plainly that a drafting habit will not fix it.
why:
Stated by the human partner 2026-09-02, watching a malformed-call slip recur a fourth time in one session: *humans and LLMs both make mistakes, and expending more effort can only reduce them so far. At some point the effort needs to go into more effective tools that prevent them or changes to the environment.*

The occasion is unusually clean evidence. The failure had been analysed down to a specific boundary within the call, the boundary was named aloud, attention was deliberately turned to it, and the next call failed at exactly that boundary — then a fifth failed while writing this memory about it. So *being careful in precisely the right place* was tried, twice, and did not work. What did work was a refusal added earlier: it left the rate untouched and turned each occurrence from a corrupted record plus a repair into a retry.

This is the general form of decisions this project had already made case by case — a vision document the model may not edit, an escape hatch kept off the tool surface so that using it needs a human act, a refusal rather than a warning. Each was argued locally; this names what they are instances of.

content: A record built for one purpose that acquires a second meaning acquires a second set of requirements nobody wrote down. The first meaning has a specification, tests and reviewers; the second has whatever was true on the day it was noticed. So defects against the second arrive one at a time, looking unrelated, each plausibly a small oversight — and they keep arriving, because there is no document to check a change against. **The tell is a field or table described in two registers**: what it is for, and what it happens to tell you. When you notice the second register, write down what it would need to be *correct* for that use, not just what it currently supplies.
context: Found 2026-08-26 on Scatterhoard. A per-record table of merge ancestry, keyed by directory, was also the only list of every location a set had ever agreed with — which made it an accidental trust record. Checkable in that project's documents/design/set-lifecycle.md under *what hangs off this list*, which gathers the four.
why: Four separate questions accumulated against one table over three weeks before anything connected them, and gathering them in one place is what showed they were all about the second meaning and none about the first. The second meaning is the dangerous one precisely because it was free: nobody chose it, so nobody owns it, and the requirements it would imply — is this key stable, does it identify what I think it identifies, when does an entry stop being true — were never asked. Writing them down is cheap at the moment the second use is noticed and expensive afterwards, because by then code depends on the accidental behaviour.

content: **When a new guard replaced a line of old code, the mutation that proves it is the old line put back, not the guard deleted.** Deleting the guard gives a third behaviour, neither old nor new, and a test for the change can pass against it — so the mutation survives and looks like a missing test when the test is fine. Seen 2026-09-24 in Scatterhoard: a guard skipping edges from superseded memories replaced a line moving those edges onto the replacement; with the guard deleted the edges stayed on the unreachable old memory, and the test passed.
context: Finishing the out-link work on Scatterhoard, recording a mutation for the walk change after the first attempt survived.
why: The obvious mutation for a guard is to remove it, and it is right when the guard was added to code that otherwise stood still. When the guard came in by rewriting a line, removing it tests an intermediate state nobody shipped. The question to ask is what the code did before the change, and to mutate back to that.

content: A name that describes how something is currently implemented, rather than the property it guarantees, is accurate only until the implementation gains an option -- and by then the name is load-bearing and expensive to change. The tell is that the name and the property coincide for a reason that is contingent: they are the same today because there is presently only one way to have the property. Name the property.
context: Found 2026-08-21 in Scatterhoard. Its `local` scope bundles a property -- not published to a repository -- with a mechanism -- lives on one machine. They coincide only because one machine is currently the only way to be unpublished, and three proposed peer-to-peer scenarios each needed the property without the mechanism. Recorded in that project's open-questions.md under the scalar-scope-form question.
why: The name reads as correct for as long as the coincidence holds, so nothing prompts a review; what forces one is a new requirement, arriving at the moment changing the name is most costly. Asking *why do these coincide* is a cheap test that can be applied while the name is still new, and it distinguishes a genuine invariant from an accident of the current design.

content: 6. Record what the habit catches: it is the only evidence the habit prevents anything. Record each time a surfaced trigger changes what the session writes, each time a session realises afterwards that a trigger should have fired, and each time one surfaced and was ignored. Record them in the project's own set, as observations linked to the trigger or lesson involved. Without them there is no telling a habit that prevents failures from one that only adds a recall to every change.
context: Writing this set's adoption guide from the decisions made while designing how projects use it, reviewed by the human partner before export.
why: Recording what the habit catches and what it misses is how its value gets measured instead of assumed; without it there is no way to tell a habit that works from one that only costs.

content: **When an artifact lives in the repository and the switch that activates it does not, the two fail independently — and testing the artifact tells you nothing about whether anyone is running it.** The clearest case is a git merge driver, and it is worth stating concretely because the abstraction hides where to look: `.gitattributes` says *use driver X for this file* and **is committed**, while `.git/config` says *driver X is this command* and **is per clone and never committed**. A fresh clone therefore gets the instruction and not the definition, and no file in the repository can supply it.
