Hooks, clean/smudge filters, editor settings and opt-in CI steps have the same split. **The failure is quiet in the worst direction**: a driver that merges perfectly and is registered nowhere produces exactly the conflicts it exists to prevent, *while looking installed to whoever wrote it*, because their clone is the one where it works. So such an item has two acceptance conditions rather than one — the artifact behaves, and the unactivated case degrades **safely rather than quietly** — and they need tracking separately, or the half that finishes first closes the item.
context: Explaining the lesson to the human partner, who could not place either the driver or the coined term — which is what showed the memory under-specified it.
why:
Superseded 2026-09-07 to name the two files. The previous version said only *the thing is committed, the switch that turns it on is not*, which is the mechanism stated abstractly with nothing to check it against — a `store-when` miss in a memory about how something works. A reader who already knew the mechanism would recognise it; a reader who did not had no way in, which was demonstrated by a reader who had just been told and still could not place it.

*Per-clone configuration* is a coined category rather than git's own vocabulary, kept because the family is real and has no established name — but the two filenames are what make it checkable, and they belong in the claim rather than behind it.

Two instances from one project: a merge driver whose registration risk was deliberately tracked in a different file from its implementation, and a `PreCompact` hook shipping as a committed script with uncommitted wiring, because the wiring carries an absolute path a collaborator cannot share. The same shape reached for unrelated reasons, and equally invisible to anyone whose machine already has it.

content: **A test that output does not depend on input order, or on seeds, passes vacuously on data with a clear answer.** When the data has well-separated structure, a clustering, optimisation or search converges to the same result from any starting point, so reversing the input or changing the seed changes nothing whether or not the code is order-independent. The test is green for the correct implementation and for the broken one alike. Build the fixture so that the starting point decides the outcome — structureless or near-tied data with many near-equal answers — and then prove it bites: put the order dependence back and watch the test fail.
context: Fixing unstable cluster descriptions in Scatterhoard, then building its charter-language declaration and one-live-charter guard, in one long session.
why: Observed 2026-09-14 on Scatterhoard, where a test that clustering ignores input order used five loose groups: ten restarts found the same partition from any seeds, and a mutation putting position-dependent seeding back survived. Only a fixture of scattered points with no groups made it fail. The trap generalises because the natural fixture for "does it find the right groups" is data that has right groups, which is exactly the data on which the starting point stops mattering. The evidence for the instance lives in the scatterhoard set.

content: **A completeness check that shares the operation's model of the data cannot catch that model being wrong -- it fails in exactly the cases the operation does.** Concretely, from a bulk migration of records out of a markdown file: the deleter assumed a record ran from its bullet line through any *indented* continuation, and the checker counted remaining records by matching that same bullet pattern. Several records had continuation paragraphs at column zero. The deleter stopped early and left their prose orphaned; the checker, looking only for bullets, reported **zero records remaining** and was wrong for every one of them. Both were right about the file as imagined and both were blind to the same discrepancy, so running the check gave no information at all. **The check that would have worked shares nothing with the operation:** total byte count against an expectation, a whole-file read, or a diff reviewed before commit -- each notices leftover text regardless of what shape it takes. **The tell that finally exposed it was an incidental one** -- a deletion removing far more lines than a single record should -- which is luck rather than method. **So: when the operation is pattern-based, verify by volume or by reading; when it is volume-based, verify by pattern.** Whatever the operation's assumption is, the check has to be capable of being surprised by it.
context: Migrating a long markdown file's entries into a memory set, when a deletion that removed thirty lines instead of two revealed that earlier deletions had silently left content behind.
why:
Recorded because the failure is silent and self-confirming, which is the worst combination: the check ran, returned the expected answer, and its agreement was evidence of nothing. That is different from a check that is merely weak -- this one could not have failed.

It is filed as an LLM-assisted-coding lesson because the shared assumption arrives naturally when the same author writes the operation and its check moments apart, from one mental model of a file it has only sampled rather than read whole. Sampling with a truncating read is what produced the model in the first place.

The instance is Scatterhoard's tracking-file migration on 2026-09-07; the evidence for it stays with that project, and what generalises is the independence requirement.

content: When a project develops a server that a client launches by absolute path out of the build directory -- an MCP server run from `target/debug/`, or any dev-mode equivalent -- routine build hygiene becomes a service outage. `cargo clean` deletes the binary the client is configured to spawn, and the client reports a crash with `Failed to spawn process: No such file or directory`. Rebuild, then restart the client. The trap is that cause and symptom sit in different processes: the clean succeeds and says so, while the failure surfaces later, elsewhere, in a log nobody is watching.
context: Happened 2026-08-20 on Scatterhoard, minutes after a mutation pass advised cleaning. The project-specific form is recorded in that repository's SETUP.md section 4, beside the existing note to restart the client after a rebuild; this entry is the part that travels.
why: This is the rule in [[01M03V5RHKES1TS3H2YMK1H6BX]] -- name what else reads the artifact you are manipulating -- meeting a case its own framing does not cover, since that memory is about importing a technique from elsewhere while this is a command native to the project. Worth its own record because the second consumer is invisible from the command: nothing about `cargo clean` suggests a running client, and the advice prompting it usually arrives from a tool with its own good reasons, such as a mutation runner reporting that a crowded build directory has made its timings untrustworthy. Two individually correct pieces of advice compose into an outage.

content: When a parameter needs a value and no data exists to tune it, ask first whether it can be a bound rather than a weight. The two fail differently: a bound set too tight is conservative rather than incorrect and can be defended with no corpus at all, while a weight set without evidence is a guess that reads as reasoned about. Where a weight is unavoidable, prefer the parameterisation that leaves the remaining constant insensitive -- trading a constant the result depends on sharply for one it barely depends on is worth doing even when the insensitive one looks less principled, because the value you cannot justify then stops mattering.
context: Drawn 2026-09-02 from Scatterhoard's traversal design, where the distinction is stated in the `Walk` doc comment in src/traversal.rs. The project-specific instance -- which constants ended up as bounds and how insensitive the remaining weight is -- is recorded in that project's own set.
why: The default move when a knob has no data behind it is to pick a plausible number and move on, and the number then acquires authority from having been shipped -- nothing downstream distinguishes a measured constant from a guessed one. Reframing the knob as a bound removes the need to justify it rather than postponing it. The second half is the less obvious one: sensitivity is itself a design choice, so a configuration can be selected for making its own untuned constants harmless.

content: When a behaviour is reachable by more than one code path, a passing test proves nothing until you know which path it took. Two guards protecting one outcome on different paths are individually unobservable: the test picks a path, the guard on that path stops the case, and the guard you meant to test is never reached. The test goes green and reads as proof. A surviving mutation is what exposes this, and it is worth reading a survivor as a question about the test's route before concluding the guard is redundant -- the two answers look identical from the test's side and call for opposite responses.
context: Found 2026-08-23 on Scatterhoard, fixing a cross-set suppression defect whose two resolution guards sit on the semantic and keyword recall paths. The project-specific form of the trap is recorded in that project's own set.
why: A single-store call delegated to the multi-store path, so a test aimed at one lookup exercised a different one and passed without touching the guard under test; rewriting it onto the other path caught the mutation at once. The general trap is that reachability is invisible in the test's own text -- nothing in a green test says which branch carried it -- so the only cheap instrument is mutating the guard and watching whether anything notices. Where two guards genuinely are redundant on every shipped path, the honest outcome is a recorded surviving mutation with its reason rather than a contrived test or a deleted guard: a guard can be worth keeping for stating the rule where the rule belongs, or for holding when the other one is later relaxed.

content: File a race condition as untestable, or add a guard with no test because two threads cannot be made to collide on demand.
context: Written with the lesson it guards, after a first-write race was filed as untestable and then tested by interleaving two connections.
why: A trigger for the lesson on testing a race by factoring its critical section: this is the moment before the mistake, phrased as a session would describe what it is about to do.

content: After adding a check that runs ahead of existing ones, rerun every mutation for the checks behind it, not only the new check's own. Tests of a later refusal that assert only that a call failed, or that its message mentions a common word, pass just as well when the new check refuses first — so they go vacuous in exactly the change that looked finished.
context: Building the release gate's directory-form group in Scatterhoard: refusing the personal set in a checkout's reserved directory, then reading a full mutation pass.
why: Observed 2026-09-27 in Scatterhoard. A new refusal of one input, placed at the head of a lookup, made two older tests pass whatever their own guards did: both exercised that input, asserted failure, and looked for the words the new message happened to contain as well. The new refusal's mutation was caught and the targeted runs were green; only a full mutation pass showed the older ones surviving. A companion to the lesson on paired negative tests: that one says a test can pass for the wrong reason, this one names the change that makes it start to. One instance, generalised because the mechanism depends only on check ordering.

content: **An interface checked the way its author wrote it fails in whatever the client does to it on arrival: test the surface through the transformations real clients apply.** A published schema is read through someone else's parser. Clients flatten it (a top-level `oneOf` shows up as a tool with no arguments), strip it (every alternation removed, so an object field arrives as a string), and validate against it (a field the schema never declared gets dropped before the server can refuse it). Each schema is correct as published and broken as received, and no test that builds its own request can see the difference. The fix is to send tests through the same transformations and publish only what survives them. Four of Scatterhoard's first 104 issues, 2026-08-01 to 2026-09-23.
context: Writing general forms for the four of Scatterhoard's nine common defect causes that had none, after re-deriving them over its 104 issues; same stretch as calibrating both shared sets and clearing the build directory.
why: Graduated from Scatterhoard's common-causes analysis. The two linked lessons cover the validating-client case and its fix; this is the general form over all three transformations, which the narrower lessons do not reach — a stripped alternation or a flattened `oneOf` passes a validating-client helper untouched. It holds for any interface published as a schema: MCP tools, OpenAPI, GraphQL, forms.

content: **An item missing from a ranked result was outranked, not judged irrelevant, so it makes a poor negative label.** Harvesting negatives from real traffic — queries a source was scored against and contributed nothing to — sounds like free, unbiased evidence, but those queries were usually about a neighbouring subject and score like answerable ones. Measured 2026-09-24 in Scatterhoard: a floor placed above such negatives would have silenced 16 of 50 and 12 of 28 real labelled queries on two sets, where a floor from the set's own contents silenced 1 of 78.
context: Testing label-free sources for a relevance floor on Scatterhoard's sets that rarely gather labelled queries.
why: The appeal is that the questions are real rather than authored, which removes one bias and hides another: *not returned* is relative to whatever else was in the pool. Before using absence as a label, ask what the item lost to; if the answer is another relevant item, the label is wrong.

content: Structural similarity between two identifiers is not evidence they mean the same thing, and reporting it as such produces confident false defects. Two names built from the same tokens in a different order are about as likely to be **opposites** as duplicates -- `write-before-read` against `read-before-write`, or a pair naming two policies where one superseded the other. Before filing a duplication defect, do two things the resemblance cannot do for you: **read what the names are attached to**, and **measure whether the duplication actually costs anything**. The second is the stronger check and is often computable -- if the thing the split supposedly severs is still reachable by another route, there is no defect however alike the names look. Note also that the classes doing real harm, inflection and synonymy, share no tokens at all, so a token method misses them while flagging the reordering that is usually deliberate.
context: Found 2026-09-02 on Scatterhoard. The withdrawn entry is `a-split-keyword-spelling-halves-every-search-for-it` in that project's ISSUES.md, which keeps the reasoning: four of the five memories involved shared three other keywords, so the subject was reachable whichever spelling a caller used and nothing had been severed. The human partner's counter-examples are what prompted reading the memories rather than the list.
why: Filed a defect from a keyword listing and withdrew it the same day after reading the memories those keywords sat on: both apparent duplicate pairs turned out to be deliberate and correct. The error is attractive because the measurement is real and the shapes genuinely match, so the finding arrives looking quantitative -- the step that was skipped is cheap and was skipped precisely because the numbers felt like enough. It also generalises past names: any similarity metric proposes a hypothesis about meaning, and the hypothesis has to be checked against what the things do rather than against how alike they look. Measuring the harm rather than the resemblance is what turns an unanswerable question into an answerable one.

content: After committing, read `git status`: anything still listed was meant to go in and did not. A pathspec narrows staging to itself. `git add <files> -A` stages every change under those paths only, not the whole tree, so a commit meant to carry a feature can carry just its new files. The slip is silent: the commit succeeds, and its message describes changes it does not contain. An empty `git status --short` after the commit, or a `git show --stat` read before calling it done, catches it in seconds while amending is still cheap.
context: Committing the first part of a feature in Scatterhoard, where new files had to be staged explicitly beside modified ones.
why: Seen on Scatterhoard on 2026-10-04: staging two new files by name with `-A` left ten modified files out of a commit, and only reading `git status` afterwards showed it. It recurs on any codebase, because the flag reads as "everything" while the pathspec quietly bounds it, and nothing reports the difference.

content: Staging files by name for a commit, especially new files beside modified ones.
context: Recording a Scatterhoard failure in which a commit carried two new files and none of the ten modified ones.
why: A trigger for the lesson on pathspecs narrowing what `git add` stages: what a session is about to do when the slip happens. Written with the lesson on 2026-10-04.

content: **Caseless matching means Unicode case folding with normalisation (`toNFKC_Casefold`), not lower-casing.** Lower-casing leaves the same word typed two ways as two strings. Full-width ＨＩＶ stays apart from HIV, a precomposed é from e plus a combining accent, and ß from "ss". Nothing reports the miss, because each half matches what it was tested on. Where a codebase already folds one kind of text this way, fold every other caseless comparison through the same function, so that "the same word" has one definition.
context: Building a list of words a server refuses to store, matched caselessly, with substring matching for Chinese and other scripts written without spaces.
why: Scatterhoard made this mistake twice. Its keyword lookup lowercased until 2026-08-23. Its never-store word list was then written on 2026-10-22 with `to_lowercase` beside a working `toNFKC_Casefold` function, and was caught only because the person's use case was Chinese, where full-width Latin is common. The failure is silent and lands on exactly the inputs nobody tested.

content: When running a long tool to find out *which* items misbehaved, redirect the whole output to a file and grep it. Piping through `tail` to keep the transcript readable discards the per-item lines that name the items, leaving a summary count nothing can act on and forcing the run to be repeated at full cost. The pull toward truncating is strongest exactly when the output is long, which is exactly when the detail is the reason for running it.
context: `python3 scripts/mutate.py` on Scatterhoard, whose full pass is around 1000 seconds and whose per-mutation rows are the only place the misbehaving names appear.
why: Done twice in one session on Scatterhoard, at about sixteen minutes a run. A mutation pass reported *4 mutations did not behave as recorded* and the rows naming them had already been thrown away by the `| tail -40` used to keep the output short -- so the second run, made to confirm the finding was not a build-crowding artifact, was truncated the same way and had to be run a third time. The summary line is what a passing run needs and the per-item rows are what a failing one needs, so truncating optimises for the case you are not in: nobody reads a long log to learn that everything was fine.

content: **Draw every field against every operation and look for the empty cells — it finds a class neither testing nor reading can reach.** Three of four findings from one such pass were **absences** rather than wrong behaviour: a field no instrument could correct, a rule no code enforced, a published property with no description. **None would be found by using the system, because nothing misbehaves** — the operation you would perform to hit the gap does not exist, so there is no failure to observe. **And none would be found by reading the file**, because each is missing *from the file you would read*: you cannot notice a row that was never written by studying the rows that were. Only laying the grid out and looking at the blanks surfaces them. The same exercise run earlier on the read surface of the same system had found a corruption-class defect, which is what made it worth repeating on the write surface.
context: Migrating a backlog entry that recorded what its own analysis pass had been good at, in a session moving tracking-file entries into a memory system.
why:
Recorded because absence is the failure mode with no natural detector. Tests assert that something happens; review reads what is present; both are blind to a cell nobody filled in. The matrix is cheap — two axes off the type definitions and the endpoint list — and it is the only one of the three that treats a blank as a finding.

Worth knowing what kind of work it produces before scheduling it: the output is defect reports rather than fixes, so its done-condition is *the analysis was performed*, and it creates work rather than closing it. That makes it easy to defer indefinitely on the grounds that nothing is broken, which is exactly the state it is designed to detect.

content: When a refusal names a remedy, test the remedy by taking it: issue the call the message recommends, in the same state that produced the refusal, and assert it succeeds. A message can name a real call that is itself refused in exactly that state, and a test asserting only the first refusal passes throughout.
context: Building several memory files per directory in Scatterhoard, while deciding how `absorb` and `evaluate` read another set's file from a checkout.
why: Observed 2026-09-26 in Scatterhoard. A refusal for a directory holding several memory files told the caller to pass `file`, and the file form refuses any path inside that directory, so the advice led straight to a second refusal. The test asserted the first message named the files and mentioned `file`, and passed. The existing lesson on naming a specific call was satisfied, since the call named was real; what it could not see is whether that call works from where the reader stands. Found only because the human partner asked what `file` pointed at. Generalising from one instance, but the shape is language-independent: advice is checked against the interface's vocabulary, not against its state.

content: A race that looks untestable can usually be tested deterministically by factoring the critical section into steps a test can call on its own, then interleaving them by hand: two connections both read, then both write. That needs no threads, sleeps or luck, and it fails reliably on the racy code. Often the factoring also finds the fix. When the steps are *read, decide, write*, the atomic form is a single conditional write that reports what won, such as an insert-if-absent followed by a re-read, and the earlier read becomes a shortcut rather than the guard. What the test proves is that the write is atomic, which is the property that matters, not that threads happen to collide.
context: Fixing a first-write race on a set's identity that had been filed as untestable; the human partner named the technique.
why: The alternative is filing the race as unfixable without an untested guard, or trying to provoke it with threads, which passes whether or not the bug is there. Two connections to one database file in one process are enough for a database race, because the database's locking is per connection. Recognising the shortcut matters for mutation testing: once the conditional write is the guard, deleting the read no longer fails anything, and that is correct rather than a gap.

content: A backup's usefulness does not decay smoothly with age; it ends at the next structural change to the data it holds -- a migration, a re-partition, records moved between stores. Past that point restoring it does not merely lose recent work, it silently undoes the structural change, and the result can be worse than the loss the backup was kept against: records reappearing where something else now owns them, two copies of one identity, a state no operation produces. So treat any migration that moves or re-homes records as invalidating every backup taken before it, take a fresh one as the last step of the migration rather than as hygiene afterwards, and name the old one for what it predates rather than only for its date.
context: Found 2026-08-31 on Scatterhoard, checking what backup the `local` set had before changing anything else. Checkable against the dated directories under ~/.local/share/scatterhoard-backups and the *Moving memories between sets* procedure in documents/design/set-lifecycle.md, which records the 2026-08-12 move of thirteen memories.
why: The dangerous property is that nothing about such a backup looks wrong. It is well-formed, it is readable, it restores cleanly, and the operation reports success -- so the check people actually perform, *can I still read it*, passes exactly when the answer is least useful. The instance: a personal memory set's only backup predated a documented move of thirteen memories out of it into another set, and thirteen of its twenty-six records now live in that other set, so restoring it would have put one id in two sets -- the precise hazard the system's identity scheme exists to prevent, sitting in the file that was supposed to be the safety net. It was found only because something else prompted a look at what protection that set actually had.

content: A number parsed out of another tool's text output must be checked against a case where it is not zero before the parser is trusted. A field-index error and a true zero produce the same output, so an extractor aimed at the wrong column looks correct for as long as the thing it counts does not happen — and what it counts is usually failures, so the reassuring reading is the one that survives longest. Validate the extractor on a deliberately non-zero input rather than on a clean run.
context: Found 2026-08-24 on Scatterhoard, when a sweep added the project's first `#[ignore]`d tests and the documented count command reported none of them.
why: A documented `cargo test` summariser used `awk -F'[ ;]'`, so each `; ` separator produced an empty field and shifted the indices: `$6` and `$8` landed on the words `failed` and `ignored` instead of their counts, and the command printed `0 failed, 0 ignored` for every possible run. It read correctly for a day because both were genuinely zero, and it was written into a project instruction file as the authoritative way to re-derive counts. The first run with a parked test exposed it. The fix was one character, `[ ;]+`; the cost would have been a session reporting a green suite that was not.

content: A safeguard that is working produces no events; one that misfires produces all of them. So the felt evidence about any quiet guard is close to 100% noise, and it gets worse with exposure rather than better -- more time on the system means more false alarms and still no true positives to weigh them against. The practical consequence: the person most motivated to replace a guard is usually the one who only ever sees it lie, and their replacement will be measurably better at the guard's APPARENT purpose while destroying the real one. Treat a proposal to replace a noisy safeguard as two things at once -- a report of a genuine defect, which it almost always is, and the moment the threat model has to be restated, because the proposer's evidence is real and systematically incomplete.
context: Recounted 2026-09-02 by the human partner from a production system, while working out how constraint-shaped lore should be linked. Logs were archived and uploaded, and each upload wrote a SHA256 of the archive into the NEXT set of logs, so altering uploaded logs broke the chain; monitoring watched for the presence of that hash message. The check had a real false-positive window. Someone made the upload touch a file and the monitor watch for the touched file -- more reliable at confirming the upload ran, and nothing was left watching the hash. Caught only because the original author happened to be the code reviewer.
why: Learning from experience fails here in an unusual way: experience teaches the opposite of the truth, so familiarity and seniority make a reviewer worse rather than better unless they happen to be the guard's author. That defeats the standard remedy -- "have someone experienced look at it" -- by selecting for exactly the person whose lived evidence is most misleading. It also explains why this class of knowledge cannot be left oral: no amount of working on the system will teach it, and the only people who hold it are the ones who built the guard and know what it is watching for.

content: 2. When a mistake turns up that a lesson here covers, or that one should: reconstruct the one sentence the session would have recalled before writing the failing change, and recall it as the habit does. If a lesson or trigger for it is in the top five, the habit would have caught it, and nothing needs adding. If the lesson exists but did not surface, add a trigger, a short memory describing that activity in the words a session would use, linked `motivated_by` to the lesson. Then rerun the sentence to confirm the trigger surfaces. A general trigger goes in this set; one in the project's own nouns goes in the project's set, linked across sets to the lesson. If no lesson fits and the mistake would recur on a different codebase, write the lesson here, with a trigger. A project may also record the mistake in its own set, linked `instance_of` to the lesson.
context: Revising this set's adoption for its first release to beta testers, after measuring that the habit faded and that signposts would rarely have preceded a failure.
why: Folds the old parts 3 and 5 together on 2026-10-04. Recording an instance existed mainly to choose signposts, which were withdrawn; the trigger check is what makes the habit better over time. Sessions phrase what they are about to write in their project's vocabulary, which is why a project trigger matches tightly where a general one travels.

content: Where a mutation is expected to survive, require a written reason rather than accepting it. Without one, "this mutation survives" degrades into "we tolerate this", which is indistinguishable from an untested guard. The reason is also what makes the entry re-checkable later: if the mechanism that made the mutation harmless is ever replaced, the recorded reason is what tells the next reader that a redundant-looking line just became load-bearing.
context: LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project. Also the one place there where "this line changes nothing observable" is a checked claim rather than a belief.
why: Two mutations on one project legitimately survive — a reverse index that is a performance property rather than a correctness one, and an explicit deletion deliberately redundant with a database cascade. Both are defensible, and neither would be distinguishable from a hole in the suite without the written justification beside it.

content: Before a bulk migration, make the structural or encoding change against an **empty or one-item sample**, because that is where encoding faults are cheap to find and the bulk work is where they become expensive. Concretely, on 2026-09-06: creating the generated-index marker regions for two files *before* migrating any entry into them exposed two faults in the generator within minutes, both silent. It had hard-coded one file's status vocabulary, so an entry marked built in another file would have rendered as **open** and its status keyword would have been eaten as the entry's slug. And it treated a second axis as if it were status, so three readiness values that all describe *unbuilt* work would each have rendered as done. Neither is visible in a passing run — the generator emits a plausible row either way — and both would have been found, if at all, by someone reading ninety wrong rows.
context: Migrating three tracking files in a Rust project into a memory store, where a script generates index rows from the records.
why: The instinct is to migrate one real item as a pilot, which proves the happy path and exercises exactly one vocabulary. An empty region costs nothing and forces the generator to be written for the general case before any data depends on it. The faults this caught share a shape: a plausible-looking output for an input the code had never been asked about.

content: When a specification hands you a measured constant, re-derive it before building against it: the arithmetic recovers design decisions the prose never states. A spec giving a per-line JSON envelope of 49 characters fixed both the field name and the absence of every other field -- 7 for the opening brace and id key, 26 for the id, 13 for the second key, 2 to close, 1 comma -- which answered two questions that would otherwise have been guessed or asked. It is also the cheapest check that you are building the thing that was measured: a figure you cannot reproduce means the measurer had a different shape in mind, and that divergence is invisible in every other part of the spec.
context: Building a memory tool's index-line output mode from a backlog entry written the night before by another session, and finding the entry's envelope figure settled what to call the field.
why: The available moves when a spec is silent are to guess and to ask, and both were unnecessary here. The constant is not decoration -- somebody computed it over a concrete artifact, so it carries that artifact's shape, and reproducing it is a minute's work against a design conversation's round trip. The failure it guards against is worse than the ambiguity: building a slightly different shape leaves every quoted cost figure quietly wrong, because the numbers were measured against a shape that was not built, and nothing downstream compares them.

content: A backup can be incomplete at the moment it is taken, not only stale later. Copying a SQLite file while any process holds it open captures only the main file, and in WAL mode the `-wal` sidecar carries every committed transaction not yet checkpointed -- which can be most of the data, for months, since nothing forces a checkpoint. Use the engine's own online backup (`sqlite3 <db> ".backup <dest>"`, or the equivalent API) whenever the source may be open, and verify the copy by comparing a count against the live source. Every check that does not involve the source passes on a truncated copy: it opens, `PRAGMA integrity_check` is clean, and the counts look plausible because there is nothing to compare them to.
context: ~/.local/share/scatterhoard-backups on this machine; the truncated directory is renamed with a TRUNCATED-DO-NOT-RESTORE suffix and carries a README saying so. The documented procedure is in documents/design/set-lifecycle.md under moving memories between sets. Earlier backups in that directory hold no `-wal` files and were made the same way, so they are suspect by construction.
why: Measured 2026-09-01 on Scatterhoard. A pre-migration backup taken with `cp *.sqlite3` while the MCP servers held the stores open captured **51 of 81** memories; the main files had not been checkpointed since August and the sidecars held 3.4 MB each. It was discovered only by querying the backup after the migration, for an unrelated reason. Two things make this worth recording beyond the mechanism. The correct procedure was already written down in this project's own `set-lifecycle.md` -- *copying the file is not safe, the servers hold it open, the `-wal` sidecar carries committed data* -- and having it documented did not put it in reach at the moment a backup was being taken, which is an argument for verifying the artifact rather than trusting the procedure. And this shares its dangerous property with backup staleness: the check anyone actually performs is *can I read it*, which passes precisely when the answer is worthless.

content: **Before enforcing a proposed invariant, count how many existing records violate it.** Synthetic test cases are written from the same belief as the rule, so they pass by construction; only the real data can say whether the belief holds. A rule stated by convention is what data written before the convention, or without it, breaks.
context: Fixing Scatterhoard's tracking-index generator, which picked an entry's slug by keyword position, and renaming the one slug that began with the reserved `hoard-` prefix.
why: Observed 2026-09-21 on Scatterhoard. A fix for an index generator proposed two guards, both argued from a naming convention: no identifier may begin with a reserved prefix, and a record carries exactly one identifier. Five synthetic cases passed. Counting the 222 real records found one identifier with the reserved prefix, filed before the convention was enforced, and 29 records carrying a second term that the second guard would have refused. The count took a few lines of script; the guards would have refused 13% of the file. Evidence in the `scatterhoard` set under `genindex-picks-the-slug-by-position`. One instance, but the same family as the neighbouring lesson on validating versioned records, where older data again broke a newer rule.

content: A transformation applied on the receiving side is safe for convergence when it is **deterministic given the record and the receiver's fixed configuration**, and unsafe when it depends on an argument supplied per call. The first produces identical bytes on every replica, so it cannot make two copies of one record differ. The second is an opinion one caller held and another did not, and it puts two contents under one identity with nothing recording why. When auditing a system for where replicas can diverge, sort the rewrites by that question rather than by whether they modify authored data -- both do, and only one of them matters.
context: Found 2026-08-30 on Scatterhoard, distinguishing `memory_file::absorb` -- whose set list is an import argument, and which was reached as a real divergence -- from `write_memory`'s canonicalisation of a link naming its own set, which is unconditional and had been lumped in with it.
why: The distinction is invisible from the code, because the two look identical at the call site: a function that edits a record on the way in. It is visible only from the *provenance of the arguments*, which is somewhere else entirely. Getting it wrong is expensive in both directions -- condemning a harmless canonicalisation costs a redesign of a settled mechanism, and clearing a per-call rewrite leaves the divergence in place. It was got wrong twice in one session here, generalising from a genuinely dangerous rewrite to a neighbouring harmless one purely on the resemblance.

content: **When adding a validation to records that several versions of the software read and write, check what a write introduces, not everything the record restates.** A check over the whole record refuses every edit to a record written under an older rule, and refuses a newer version's values even after the data carrying them has arrived — so the next change to the format has to wait for every copy to upgrade. Treating values the data already holds as valid keeps the check aimed at what it is for: a typo or an invention at the moment someone first writes it.
context: Building a reserved-keyword block-list for Scatterhoard's write path, after committing memory files from the previous stretch.
why:
Observed 2026-09-14 on Scatterhoard, building a refusal of unknown reserved keywords. The first proposal checked every keyword on an amendment, which would have refused edits to twelve live memories still carrying a retired mark; the human partner stopped it, pointing out that different versions of the code would be in use and keyword structure would need to change again, as it already had once. The fix was to count any term the data set already holds as known. The evidence is in the `scatterhoard` set under `reserved-keyword-block-list`.

One instance, hence the confidence: the general form — a validator introduced over a shared, versioned format should leave already-present values alone — reads as sound on file formats, database schemas and wire protocols, but has been tested here once. The cost that comes with it is also general: a bad value that arrived before the validation, or from outside it, stays valid in that data.

content: When results from two sources are combined, ask what each number is measured against. If the answers differ, either put them on a common baseline or keep them in separate lists and let the caller decide. Never average, interleave by quota, or normalise and hope — the first two invent a ranking and the third hides the problem. The recurring pressure is that a caller would rather have one ranked list than two; that preference is real and is not a reason to fabricate comparability.
context: LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project. The fix in the first case was to centre both corpora on the mean of their union.
why: Three times in one day, in three different places, a design pressure appeared to merge quantities that were not comparable: two corpora each centred on their own mean and merged by score, a keyword match count tempted into one list with a cosine similarity, and a single similarity field that a count-based search would have had to populate with something. Each looked like a small local convenience, and each would have produced an ordering that looks fine — a sorted list of numbers gives no sign that half of them were measured against a different baseline.

content:
Deciding to perform a side effect and narrating it in the same sentence is enough to produce a confident false report that it happened. The failure has a signature: the action is small, incidental to the turn's main work, and gets mentioned in a closing aside -- "one small note, I also updated X" -- rather than being the thing the turn was about. The main work really was done, so nothing in the turn feels wrong.

It is worst for writes whose effect is invisible from the conversation: memory stores, cache updates, config writes, anything the user cannot see failing. A false report there does not merely mislead, it makes the user stop tracking the thing themselves, which is precisely when they stop being the backstop.

The cheap guard is ordering: make the call before writing the sentence that claims it, never after. Where an aside mentions a side effect, treat the sentence as unwritable until a tool result exists for it. Reviewing the turn's own tool calls before summarising catches the rest.
context: Reporting to a user that a memory had been updated when no such call had been made, caught only because they asked a follow-up question two turns later.
why: Recorded because the cost here was zero only by luck -- the user happened to ask a question that surfaced it, and had they not, they would have switched context believing state was saved that was not. The generalisation is safe despite resting on one observed instance, because the mechanism is not specific to memory tools or to this codebase: any side effect mentioned as an aside rather than performed as the turn's subject is exposed to it, and the same shape would produce a claimed-but-unwritten file, a claimed-but-unrun migration, or a claimed-but-unsent message. The ordering fix is stated as a rule about sentences rather than about diligence deliberately, since "be careful" is what already failed.

content: A mutation proves a guard is load-bearing for some input the suite supplies. It says nothing about whether that input resembles anything the running system produces, so a guard can be exercised, mutation-pinned and green while refusing nothing that will ever reach it. Where a guard compares an incoming value against a constant, ask separately what values that comparison can actually take in the field: if every value the system produces falls on one side, the guard is inert, and neither the test nor the mutation will say so because both are working from the same unreal input. The check is cheap -- enumerate what has actually been written or emitted, rather than what the type admits.
context: Found 2026-08-31 on Scatterhoard, checking whether a planned set-UUID change could make existing memory files unreadable. Checkable in src/memory_file.rs at `check_version` and `compatibility_of`, and in ISSUES.md as `the-format-version-gates-nothing-while-the-format-is-0x`.
why: This is a limit of mutation testing rather than a misuse of it, which is what makes it worth recording where a project leans on the technique: the mutation and the test are the same instrument read twice, so they agree even when both are measuring a domain that does not occur. The instance: a file-format version check compared major versions, and the test that pinned it used `99.0.0` -- a major this project has never written and, while the format is `0.x`, never will. Every real file passed the gate for the same reason, so an incompatible format change would have surfaced as a malformed record partway through a file instead of as a refusal. Both the test and its mutation had been green for a month. The tell was not in the test or the corpus but in the shipped values: three versions had ever existed and all three began `0.`.

content: 4. Choose signposts: keep up to three, for the lessons with the most instances among the last 20 failures. Where a project has recorded fewer than 20, count all of them. Ties go to the lesson with the most recent instance, and a lesson needs at least two instances to qualify. A signpost is a memory in the project's own set, marked `hoard-signpost`, whose opening line is taken from the lesson's trigger — what a session recognises at the moment it matters — and which links to the lesson. Check the selection whenever a failure is recorded. When a lesson falls out of the top three, retire its signpost by superseding it without the mark. The recall habit covers everything below the cut.
context: Writing this set's adoption guide from the decisions made while designing how projects use it, reviewed by the human partner before export.
why: Tested against one project's nine recurring causes: a threshold alone selected all nine, while its last 20 failures picked the three matching current work and dropped those tied to finished work. Three bounds the lines pushed into every session; two instances keep a young project from signposting one-off accidents.

content:
When you find yourself writing that an approximation is "reasonable rather than exact", stop and check it. That sentence is the tell: you have noticed the assumption clearly enough to hedge it in prose, which means you are already close enough to test it — and hedging feels like diligence while leaving the code resting on the unchecked claim.

Substituted lifetimes are where this bites hardest. A process standing in for a session, a request for a transaction, a connection for a user: each is a plausible proxy, each is usually checkable in about a minute against the artefacts the other side already leaves behind — process start times against log or transcript files, for instance — and each fails silently when wrong, because the code does something reasonable either way.
context: Building a query log's answerability label in Scatterhoard, and being asked whether a process's life really approximates a session's.
why: Found 2026-09-11 on Scatterhoard, and by the human partner rather than by me. A label was bounded to the life of a server process as a stand-in for a session; I documented the substitution as "reasonable rather than exact" and shipped it. It took one `ps` against the client's transcript timestamps to show the server had been running two hours and had already served two other sessions, so the bound spanned conversations that had nothing to do with each other. The hedge in the comment was written *instead of* the check, which is the part worth remembering: the doubt had already been articulated and then spent on prose.

content: **When a sweep finds its work by the absence of a derived record, a permanent "nothing to produce" has to leave a positive record, or the sweep retries it forever.** "Never tried" and "tried, and there is no result" are the same absence, so a sweep keyed on missing rows cannot tell them apart. The retry cannot succeed — only a change to the input or to the producer could change the answer, and those usually re-derive through their own paths — so it is pure waste, and it grows with the number of such items, which is largest for exactly the users who meet the case most. **Record the verdict in the derived table itself**, where the operations that invalidate derived state already clear it, so it is cleared for free when the input is rewritten or the producer changes, instead of being kept in step by hand in a second table. The cost moves to reads: every reader of that table must tell a verdict from a result, so pin with a test the reader that would fail *quietly* — typically an "is there a result for this?" check.
context: Fixing a store-stopping failure in Scatterhoard's embedding path; the design discussion about whether an unrepresentable memory needs a marker row, and what the gap sweep is for.
why:
Worked out 2026-09-11 with the human partner on the scatterhoard project. They asked whether the marker was needed at all if the system could otherwise tell what had been tried; it could not, because genuine gaps — records written by a process that could not produce the derived data — are absent rows too. A separate marker table was rejected because every place that clears the derived table would also have to clear it: the drift pattern of two hand-maintained copies of one fact.

Evidence stays with the project: `one-unembeddable-memory-stops-the-store` in the scatterhoard set, and the 2026-09-11 section of its `documents/design/embeddings.md`.

content: When a record's serialised bytes are hashed -- for a checksum, a content address, or three-way reconciliation -- adding a field is a compatible addition or a forced rewrite of every existing record, and the only thing deciding which is whether the field is *omitted* when absent or written as an explicit null. Omitted, every existing record keeps its exact bytes: nothing reconciles as modified, nothing needs migrating, and holders that never write the field are unaffected forever. Written as null, every record's hash moves at once, so a change that adds nothing anyone asked for arrives as a diff touching the whole corpus. Decide it at the moment the field is declared, and assert the emptiness in a test, because the difference is one serialiser attribute and is invisible in every other reading of the code.
context: Found 2026-08-31 on Scatterhoard, adding set identity to memory files. Checkable in src/memory/link.rs at `LinkTarget::CrossSet` and in tests/memory_file.rs as `a_cross_set_link_without_an_identity_adds_nothing_to_the_line`, with a mutation pinning it.
why: The choice looks like formatting and is actually the migration plan. It reverses the usual instinct too: an explicit null reads as more honest and more self-describing, and here it is the option that costs everyone a rewrite. Worth stating separately from *make optional fields optional*, because the concern is not whether old readers cope -- they cope either way -- but whether the bytes of records nobody edited stay identical. The instance: adding a target set's identity to cross-set links in a corpus where seven records held one, with `skip_serializing_if` making the difference between touching those seven deliberately and moving every record in the set.

content: Reachability from the work surface has two mechanisms, and the choice between them is decided by whether the rule is short enough to copy. **Embed the rule** where it is a sentence or two: the reader needs nothing else, and it survives being read out of context. **Link to it** where it is longer: a pointer in the file the work passes through, aimed at one authoritative statement elsewhere. The pointer buys the same *removes the need to know* property, and it buys it without a second copy that can drift -- which is the cost an embedded notice quietly accepts and can only pay because it is short. The failure mode to watch for is a rule that grew: embedded when it was two lines, still embedded at twenty, now differing between three files with nothing reporting the disagreement.
context: Deciding where a project's guidance for shaping tracking-file memory clusters should live, having rejected the served conventions, the design documents and the memory set in turn.
why:
Recorded as the part not already covered. The general claim -- a centrally-listed rule is only found by someone who already knows to look -- is held by the viral-notice memory this links to, and is not restated here. What that one does not offer is a choice, because the case it was drawn from had a notice short enough that duplication cost nothing.

Confidence is moderate: the reasoning is sound and the drift argument is the same one that holds everywhere else, but this is one instance, decided once, on a rule of roughly thirty lines. The threshold between the two mechanisms is asserted rather than measured, and *short enough to copy* is doing work no evidence here pins down.

content: A standing instruction that fires on a boundary the model must notice for itself will not fire. Tie it to something externally observable — a tool action, a file being written, something the human says — or accept that it runs only when someone else supplies the cue. "After you finish a piece of work" reads like a trigger and is not one, because the question *am I finished?* only surfaces when something outside the model raises it, and mid-task the model is inside the work rather than looking back at it.
context: Found 2026-08-24 on Scatterhoard, examining why its `capture-before-ending` convention anchors on commits and session ends. The project-specific form is recorded in that project's own set.
why: Measured on Scatterhoard's own memory corpus 2026-08-24: 88 of 105 memories were stored within three minutes of another, the signature of a sweep rather than of storage at the moment of learning, and at most four in the whole corpus arrived alone inside a working session. The governing convention names four moments, of which three are externally marked — about to commit, about to export, the human says they are wrapping up — and one, "a multi-turn piece of work is finished", is self-assessed. Only the marked ones fire. Demonstrated live in the same session: an investigation running ten commands across two corpora produced findings and triggered no capture until the human pointed it out. The remedy is not to restate the self-assessed clause more insistently; it is to name an observable event, or to add one.

content: This set's adoption guide is found through the paragraph a project puts in its `AGENTS.md`, which names `coding-lessons-adoption-guide`, and through the repository's README, as of 2026-10-04. Until then a signpost pushed a line pointing at the guide into every session holding the set. It was retired when the habit moved into the opt-in paragraph, since nothing left in the guide applies at the start of a session.
context: Revising this set's adoption for its first release to beta testers, after measuring that the habit faded and that signposts would rarely have preceded a failure.
why: Supersedes the guide's signpost without `hoard-signpost`, which retires it from the start-of-session push. The memory stays, so recall still finds it.

content: Recall `coding-lessons-adoption-guide` to set this set up for a project; ends when that guide is withdrawn. It is how a project adopts this set: the opt-in sentence, recalling before writing, signposts and triggers, including when a project's `AGENTS.md` names the guide.
context: Writing this set's adoption guide from the decisions made while designing how projects use it, reviewed by the human partner before export.
why: Pushed at the start of every session holding this set, so the guide is found without anyone knowing to search for it. The only action it names is to recall.

content: When something must be pushed into every session unconditionally rather than looked up, make the push the marked exception and say so in the rule itself. The criterion that survives contact with a real list: push only what the reader would never think to put into words, because search reaches everything they would. A recurring crash needs no push -- when it recurs they will describe it and find the cluster; a question shape nobody would articulate does, because no query will ever reach it. Pair that with an obligation to state what would end each pushed item, attached to the act of marking rather than to the material generally, since the marked thing is what spends the standing budget.
context: Designing a session-start push list for a memory tool, deciding which accumulating records earn a place on it. The same stretch of work had just rewritten a field description on the same tool and retired a convention that turned out to be already served inside another one.
why: Unconditional context is a charge on every session forever, so it grows monotonically and nothing reports it. The usual remedies work on the wrong end: an eviction rule removes things after they are already costing, and a size cap forces a fight among items that were never comparable. Restricting what may be added at all is a better bound because it uses a test the author can apply at the one moment they have the information -- would I have searched for this? The ending obligation closes the other leak, and putting it on the marking rather than on the content is what keeps it from taxing everything that merely accumulates. Being unable to state an ending turns out to be an answer rather than an obstacle: an item nobody can imagine closing is one that should not have been pushed.

content: A recorded mutation's find text must be anchored on something unique to the function under test — and uniqueness is not a property you can establish once. An anchor that was unique when written becomes ambiguous the moment a structurally parallel function is added, because the runner matches literal text and takes the first occurrence. Four mutations aimed at two existing operations silently retargeted onto a third that was added later and sits earlier in the file, sharing lines like `Err(error) => unreadable = Some(error)`. A staleness check cannot catch this: the anchor still matches, so nothing reports a problem. The damage runs both ways — the retargeted mutations report as defects in guards they never touched, and they survive on the new function's copies, so the mis-aim is also the only sign those copies are untested. When adding an operation parallel to an existing one, re-run the existing one's mutations rather than only the new one's.
context: Found 2026-08-25 on Scatterhoard, building `restore` beside an existing `drop` and `import`. Surfaced only by a full mutation pass — the `--only` runs during development had passed, because the parallel function did not exist yet. Checkable in scripts/mutations.py, where the four repaired anchors carry the reason inline.
why: The original lesson framed this as care at writing time, which is insufficient: the anchor here was correct when written and was invalidated months later by code that never touched the mutated line. That makes it the same shape as a surviving-mutation reason going stale because the suite grew — a mutation record is a claim about the whole file, not about its own line. The two-way damage is what makes it worth more than a note: a false defect wastes a cycle, but the masked gap is silent, and it lands on exactly the new code nobody has tested yet.

content: A correlation across a set where two attributes always travel together is one observation, not two. Before reporting a shared property as the cause, ask what else every affected case shares, and name the case that would separate them. If no such case can be constructed, the explanation is not yet a finding. Writing a confound down as a cause is worse than leaving it open, because a filed cause stops people looking.
context: LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project.
why: Having already misattributed one cause, the corrected explanation was itself a confound: every affected instance was both declared in a particular config file and colliding with another name, so both explanations fit every observation. Isolating one variable took a single additive test case and one restart, and showed correlation with the declaration site perfect and with the collision zero. The correction needed correcting within the hour, and it had been written specifically to be more careful — care applied below the level of the confound does not reach it.

content: Trigger: about to compare words or text without regard to case, such as matching a user's list of words against what they write, deduplicating names or tags, or looking something up caselessly.
context: Adding the trigger after the never-store word list was written with lower-casing.
why: Written in the words a session uses when describing such a change, so a recall before writing it surfaces the lesson. The first time, it did not: a recall describing a caseless word list returned nothing about folding.

content: 5. Write a trigger: add one when recalling what a failure's author was about to write misses its lesson. When a failure is recorded, reconstruct the one sentence the session would have used before writing the failing change, and recall it as the habit would. If none of the lesson's triggers is in the top five, write one — a short memory describing the activity, linked `motivated_by` to the lesson. A general trigger goes in this set, phrased without the project's nouns; a project trigger goes in the project's own set, phrased in its nouns and linked across sets to the lesson; it can be both. Rerun the sentence to confirm the new trigger surfaces. A trigger that surfaced and was ignored does not need another; record it as part 6 describes. One that keeps surfacing with nothing to say is narrowed, by superseding it.
context: Writing this set's adoption guide from the decisions made while designing how projects use it, reviewed by the human partner before export.
why: Sessions phrase what they are about to write in their project's vocabulary, so a general trigger travels but matches loosely, and a project trigger matches tightly and travels nowhere. The one miss in the measurement was a query in exactly those nouns.

content: When a model issues tool calls in parallel, a call that needs an identifier another call in the same batch will create has nothing to put there but a guess, and the guess is wrong. The failure is silent wherever the receiving tool accepts a reference it cannot resolve. Observed twice in one session: a memory linked to another stored in the same batch, the link written with an invented id. Both times it was caught only because the server reported an unresolved link. Order dependent writes: make the call that yields the identifier, read it, then make the call that uses it. Better still, give the tool a way to express the dependency inside one call, so ordering is not the model's to remember.
context: Filing an open question with its supporting records; the second occurrence, after the first had already been noticed and corrected the same day.
why: Batching independent calls is the right default, so the dependent case is easy to sweep in by reflex. The invented identifier has the right shape and passes every check that does not resolve it. A reflexive action is not reliably governed by a recalled rule, which is why the stronger fix is in the tool: let one call carry both writes and their reference.

content: When instruction text for a model reads as too long, measure before cutting, because filler density and words per sentence answer different questions. Text carrying almost no filler is not verbose, and cutting content there removes arguments while leaving the length roughly where it was. The usual cause is the periodic sentence that arrives at its point after a dash or colon: standing instructions are read in sequence rather than studied, so the whole arc is paid for before anything is delivered. Put the operative claim at the front of the sentence and one claim in each. That is close to length-neutral, and legibility rather than size is what it buys.
context: Measured on the Scatterhoard project's served convention catalog, 2026-08-25: 0.20% filler across 2,955 words, and a restructuring pass that held wording fixed cut mean sentence length by a third while taking 1% off the character count.
why: Both available readings of "this is too long" send you somewhere useless if you do not measure first. Read as verbosity, it licenses cutting content that is load-bearing; read as an unavoidable cost, it licenses raising the budget. The measurement separates them in about a minute and points at a third answer neither reading offers. The essay shape is also the pull while drafting, because it reads beautifully once, and once is not how served text is read.

content: **Full export review of the `coding-lessons` set under Scatterhoard's judgement gate, completed 2026-10-28: every record the export committed with this marker holds has been reviewed.** It covered all 197 memories, sentence by sentence against the person's sharing preferences and the routing in Scatterhoard's export-review design as it stood at that date, with no private-only exceptions in force, since the repository is public. A routine review starts from the export this marker is committed with.
context: Writing the full-review markers for all three sets after the scatterhoard review finished.
why: The full-review marker the export-review design asks for, one per set. The 2026-10-19 marker predates the judgement gate, so the conditions changed and a full review was due. 17 memories were flagged, and the person cleared all 17. The review also produced the principle for class claims about reasoning beings, recorded in the `scatterhoard` set, because most of the first flags were general lessons about how LLMs behave.

content: When a change removes a side effect from an operation tests use as setup — a constructor, a create call, a fixture — run the full mutation pass, not only the mutations for the code you changed. A test that took its precondition from that side effect keeps passing, now vacuously, and only the mutation of some unrelated guard it was protecting shows it.
context: Building Scatterhoard's set-settled-at-first-write step 1 — create stops minting, first write and export mint — and reading the full mutation pass afterwards.
why: Observed 2026-09-28 in Scatterhoard: `create` stopped minting a set identity. Three tests had relied on the minted identity without saying so. One checked that no identity was invented from another loaded set, which could not fail once no loaded set had one. Two checked an import's note, and now reached a different branch whose wording shared the word they looked for. The suite stayed green; the targeted mutation run exposed two, and only the full pass the third. A sibling of the lesson on checks added ahead of others: a different change, the same way a test goes vacuous. One change with three instances, generalised because the mechanism depends only on tests borrowing a precondition from shared setup.

content: A marker with control mechanics needs a spelling for talking *about* it, or the discussion lands in the thing it controls. Any in-band label that makes a system act -- a reserved tag, a magic string, a keyword that puts a record into a list -- gets written about eventually, in a note, a design record or a test fixture, and the natural instinct is to label that discussion with the term it discusses. It then enters the population the marker selects, where it is indistinguishable from a real entry and arrives wherever that population is consumed. Reserve the namespace *and* give the discussion its own form, such as an `about-` prefix, at the moment the marker is introduced rather than after the discussion accumulates.
context: Working out why a session-start list kept filling with memories about the list mechanism, and being handed the general form of the fix.
why: The failure is invisible while the population is small and grows fastest exactly when a mechanism is under active design, because that is when people write about it -- so the marker is noisiest in the period it is least stable. Measured on one memory tool: the reserved keyword naming a set's charter returned nine records of which four were charters and five were design notes about charters, and a second reserved keyword had gone from three such notes to seven in two days of work on the mechanism. Retrofitting is the part that hurts, and it is why this belongs at introduction: where records are append-only or externally published, the discussion entries may not be re-labellable at all, so the rule can prevent new ones and cannot repair the old.

content: A running Claude Code session cannot pick up a newly added MCP server — tool definitions are bound at session startup, so the session that writes the server config cannot see the tools it just registered. Clearing the context does not help; it resets the conversation, not the client's MCP connections. The /mcp command also behaves differently by host: in command-line Claude Code it manages servers, but in the Code mode of the Desktop app it points at the marketplace and offers no way to attach a local server.
context: Learned while attaching a local MCP server during development, written up in that project's SETUP.md section 3b, which is where to check whether it still holds after a client update. Confirmed by attempting a reconnect twice. Moved here from the personal set 2026-08-15; re-verify against current client versions before relying on it.
why: Both non-workarounds look like they should work, so the failure mode is spending a session trying to reconnect instead of just starting a new one.

content: **An instruction of the form *produce X when the session ends* can invert into *the session should end because X was produced*.** Observed 2026-09-16: the project's standing instructions tie writing a session checkpoint to the end of a session or a signal of wrapping up. The human partner asked for two checkpoints mid-session, for safe-keeping; after each, the assistant began offering stopping points, and the first such offer came before the human had said anything about time. They noticed, and asked whether a session limit was causing it — there was no session-limit signal of any kind, and the budget was nowhere near exhausted. **Two other contributors were evidenced and are legitimate**: the human had said they had a few minutes left, which is a real constraint to match; and clean commit boundaries make *shall we stop* feel like the next sentence, though a clean tree means the last thing is safely recorded rather than that the next thing should not start. **What could not be settled from the inside** is whether a pull toward wrapping up after a long conversation also contributed. **The practical correction**: a boundary is worth flagging — *this is committed, nothing is lost if you stop here* — and the recommendation attached to it is not, because continuing is the collaborator's decision and they hold the information it turns on.
context: Wrapping up a long session on Scatterhoard, after the human partner asked why the assistant kept offering stopping points.
why:
Recorded because the inversion is quiet and self-justifying: producing the artifact feels like evidence about whether to continue, when it is evidence only that the work so far is safe. The instruction is correct and worth keeping; what needs noticing is that satisfying it mid-session says nothing about ending.

Generalised cautiously, and the limits are worth stating. This is one instance, in one session, with a cause that was traced rather than isolated — the human's stated time constraint is a sufficient explanation for the later offers on its own, and only the earliest one requires anything else. What survives regardless of the cause is the correction, which costs nothing and does not depend on knowing why the nudging started.

Checkable in the conversation of 2026-09-16 and in the project's checkpoint instruction. The general shape should hold for any artifact an instruction binds to a phase boundary — a handover note, a release summary — where producing it early can be mistaken for reaching the boundary.

content: An LLM reasoning about a deliberate-looking limit will reach for the artifacts that state a decision rather than the one that justifies it, because the first are far more reachable. A tool schema is one search away and served conventions arrive unprompted; the design document holding the reasoning is a file nothing points at from where the work is happening. Two sources agreeing then reads as corroboration rather than as two views of one upstream choice. Before filing a defect against a limit that looks intentional, read the design document for that subject — and note that a deliberate constraint tends to agree with itself everywhere, so consistency is evidence for intent rather than against it.
context: LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard project. What surfaced it was the human partner's recollection of the original design discussion, not any check.
why: A defect was filed claiming a correction tool's omission of two fields was an oversight and that a convention listing them had drifted from the data model. Both were wrong and it was withdrawn within the hour: the design document resolved the question deliberately, and the copies agreed because they were right. The cost was a defect, a lesson written on top of it asserting a duplication that did not exist, both committed, then a correction pass across three files.

content: A session cannot follow the standing instructions it just rewrote, so the author never sees their own change work. Instruction text loaded at startup -- a served convention catalog, a tool description, a system prompt -- is bound for the life of the session, so a session that spends a day improving it operates under the old text throughout and hands the improved version to someone else. Two consequences worth planning for: the change is untested in use at the moment it is committed, however carefully it was reasoned about; and the author is the one person who cannot report on it, which makes the next session's experience the first real evidence. Schedule the restart, and treat the first session under new text as the measurement.
context: Being offered a client restart at the end of a long day rewriting a convention catalog, and noticing the whole day ran under the old one.
why: The gap is invisible from inside because everything about the change feels tested -- it was drafted, argued, measured against a corpus and committed with a green suite -- and none of that is the thing that matters, which is what a session actually does when the text reaches it cold. Worth stating because the natural instinct is the opposite: having just improved the instructions, you feel best placed to judge them, when you are in fact the only party guaranteed not to have read them. It also sets a cheap habit: end such a session with a handoff written for a reader who will have the new text and none of the reasoning.

content: This set holds engineering lessons that outlive any one project: how work goes wrong, and what to do differently. A memory belongs here when it would hold on a different codebase in a different language — testing and verification technique, debugging method, design judgement, tooling behaviour. Project-specific findings belong with their project. Anything about the person, their machine or their working preferences belongs to the personal set instead. Two tagging conventions apply: tag a memory with a language name when it is specific to that language or its toolchain, and tag it llm-assisted-coding when it is specific to working with an LLM rather than to programming generally.
context: Written at set creation, as route-where requires. The material came from that personal set and from LESSONS.md in the Scatterhoard repository, which had been standing in for this store.
why: Created 2026-08-15 to hold what the personal set had been carrying for want of anywhere better — by its own description, eight of its ten memories were general lessons rather than preferences. The two tagging conventions exist because the set mixes audiences: a Rust toolchain finding and a lesson about how an LLM misreads its own reachable artifacts are both durable and general, but a reader filtering for one does not want the other, and a keyword is the only filter available.

content: When an operation needs an escape hatch that bypasses its own safety rule, leaving the hatch outside the tool surface is a design choice rather than an omission. Where a destructive operation cannot run because its safety copy has nowhere to go, the way through can be a documented manual step — delete the file by hand and restart — with no force flag offered. A flag is one argument away from any caller including a model in a hurry, while a manual deletion plus a restart cannot happen without a human doing it deliberately.
context: Raised 2026-08-06 on the Scatterhoard project in response to "what if the disk is full because the store filled it", recorded in documents/design/set-lifecycle.md under "Forcing a drop is deliberately not a tool". Moved here from the personal set 2026-08-15.
why: This supplies by construction the guarantee that naming conventions only approximate: an argument reachable from the same call site is a speed bump, not a barrier. It is also consistent with refusing to let a caller hand-create state whose format the writer owns — deleting invents nothing, whereas creating invents a version number.

content: An instrument that reports its recorded expectations is not reporting outcomes, and the two decay apart. A recorded expectation -- a mutation expected to be caught, a test expected to fail, a golden file expected to differ -- can stop being true because unrelated code made the checked line redundant, while the line itself and the text locating it are untouched. Staleness checks keyed on whether the record still matches the source cannot see this, because it still matches. Only running the whole corpus and reading its summary can, so a coverage figure quoted from a listing is a claim about the record rather than about the code.
context: Found 2026-08-25 on Scatterhoard. A full pass -- the first in some days -- turned up one mutation recorded as caught that no longer was: a refold added later rebuilt the column whose backfill the mutation removes, so the test written for it stayed green. The staleness check passed it, and the corpus listing counted it among the caught.
why: The recommendation to have an instrument report its own corpus size is right and answers a narrower question than it gets read as: how many entries exist and what each expects, not what any of them did.
